justification: The refugee solicitudes increased by 4.5 % in comparison with 2022 first three months. However the levels of application are still low because of knowledge about the refugee system application

subindicator: ILS2.2 - Accessible, safe and accurate information
justification:
A survey of affected people and interviews with humanitarian practitioners in Haiti revealed that humanitarian presence and access issues were obscure to many affected people, who lacked information on what aid was available and what was preventing it
from getting to where it is needed.

The Kremlin mass media and Telegram Z-channels are spreading a video showing an Orthodox church set on fire. Russian propagandists claim that this church is part of the Ukrainian Orthodox Church of Moscow Patriarchate (UOC MP), situated in the Mykolaiv region’s village of Novopavlivka, and has allegedly been set on fire by some ‘separatists’ or ‘security forces’.
The Kremlin media and Russian Telegram channels are spinning false information about the alleged preparation for the mass mobilization of Ukrainian women.

Russian Telegram channels shared online advertising platform screenshots. The publication informs that an apartment is for rent in Lviv. In the description states "if the city's territory is transferred to the jurisdiction of another state, a lessee is obliged to fulfill his/her obligations in full under the current lease agreement." There is a caption below that renting this apartment is a "unique opportunity to move to Europe in one day." and the photo with Polish flag reading "Ready to return Lviv".
It turned out that the photos show an apartment located not in Lviv but in Moscow.

Russian shares fake news about Ukraine allegedly reselling ambulance donated by Poland. The information about the donated ambulance put up for sale has proven to be fake. This became obvious from the original post, which was found via the Google image search.

Z-Telegram channels and Twitter bots share the "cover" of the Handelsblatt German business daily. The photo shows a caricature of President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky who is not allowed to join NATO.

Russian fake: Poles being prepared for nuclear accident. Propagandists forged the radiation emergency instructions of the Ministry of Health of Poland. There are no radiation emergency instructions on the official website of the Ministry of Health of Poland, as well as on its official Facebook page. Such instructions were not printed, the Ministry representatives told Ukrinform.

Russian propaganda faked an episode of the national news telethon. "Ukraine will build concentration camps for Russians", "Verkhovna Rada is preparing a ‘law’ on sending Russian soldiers to labor camps" – the Kremlin media outlets and pro-Russian Telegram channels spread messages with such headlines.

Russian propaganda continues to fabricate content to discredit Ukrainians abroad.
In their posts, Russian Telegram channels began to actively share a photo of a memorial plaque to composer Richard Wagner in Dresden. According to propagandists, it was allegedly defaced by Ukrainian vandals who wrote the word "Orc" on the wall near the plaqu

Russian Telegram channels, VKontakte social media pages and pro-Kremlin media outlets have spread a video, which shows Chief of the Main Intelligence Directorate at the Ukrainian Defense Ministry Kyrylo Budanov giving an interview to journalist Dmytro Komarov and speaking of the alleged plans for the physical destruction of about 3 million residents of the temporarily occupied Crimea. Russian propagandists have combined different extracts from a video interview with the chief of the Ukrainian intelligence, Kyrylo Budanov

During June 20-22, Russian media spread a fake that the wife of the President of Ukraine Olena Zelenska had Israeli citizenship. This allegedly indicates the preparation of the president’s family for escape from Ukraine. A photocopy of the first page of the first lady’s Israeli passport was presented as “evidence.” However, the falsification turned out to be of really low quality. As a basis, the creators of the fake took a template of an Israeli passport, which can be easily found on the Internet.

Fake: The Russians destroyed five Patriot complexes in Ukraine

Fact: Putin announced the destruction of more systems than Ukraine has. Ukraine regularly receives ammunition for Patriot in military aid packages from the United States, which indicates the successful combat use of these complexes by the Armed Forces of Ukraine.

On June 28, Chair of the Federation Council of Russia Valentina Matvienko stated that a report of the commission to investigate the activities of American biological laboratories in Ukraine had been sent to all parliaments of the world. The document refers to the development of “combat” mosquitoes, ticks and lice, “experiments on the military” and “pumping soldiers with drugs.”
Fake: Americans are breeding combat insects in Ukraine and drugging the Ukrainian military.

Fact: The Russian parliament is promoting evidence-free conspiracy at the international level.

subindicator: ILS4.4 - Deliberate communication shutdowns / restrictions from malicious actors
justification: Ethiopia's telecoms and internet dominance has been used to suppress groups, hide war crimes, and suppress human rights violations. In Tigray, Ethiopia, the government has implemented the longest continuous internet shutdown in the world since 2020, keeping Tigrayans isolated amid a war that has cost their livelihoods and lives.

International rights organizations Amnesty International and the Committee to Protect Journalists have called on Ethiopia to stop arbitrarily arresting journalists and respect citizens' right to peaceful protests. The groups urged Ethiopian authorities to release seven journalists and drop all charges, investigate allegations of physical assault, and protect the right to freedom of expression and peaceful protest.

The House of Peoples' Representatives approved the New Media Law on February 2, 2021, bringing hope for a better repressive environment. Under the EPRDF, journalists and media personnel faced human rights violations like torture, arrest, detention, and intimidation. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed pledged to transition the country into a democracy by opening political space and ensuring freedom of expression in 2018.

Nine journalists and media workers working for Nisir International Corporation and Ashara, both Youtube Channels in Ethiopia’s northern Amhara region, were arrested when local authorities raided the offices of the two media outlets on 19 and 20 May and confiscated media equipment.

Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government has arrested over 4,500 people in the Amhara region, including 18 journalists and YouTubers. The purge, targeting politicians, members of the influential Amhara nationalist militia, and journalists, has led to the arrest of some still secretly held by authorities.

Arrests and harassment of journalists, opposition figures and activists in Ethiopia have risen this year, the war-torn country’s rights watchdog said, underlining “concerning” levels of violence despite a peace agreement.

The Ethiopian Human Rights Commission (EHRC) report on the year to June noted “an increase in the arrest and harassment of media personnel, members of opposition political parties and civil society groups, raising concerns on the shrinking of civic space”.

subindicator: ILS2.2 - Accessible, safe and accurate information
justification: Information in emergencies and communication with affected people has long been recognised as vital for effective humanitarian response. This appears to be lacking in the Haiti response, as affirmed by interviewees, and evidenced by a pattern of responses in our survey. The proportion of people responding “I don’t know” to questions about their understanding of the aid response and the obstacles to access were markedly higher than in other challenging contexts surveyed for this research programme.

subindicator: ILS2.2 - Accessible, safe and accurate information
justification: Other diversity factors among mixed migration flows are related to language, where 18.9% of respondents between Ciudad Juarez and Tapachula confirm facing barriers to communicate in Spanish. 5.6% of people indicated having significant or total difficulty. There is an insufficient offer of interpretation services in official processes and in assistance projects in both locations, which prejudices these individuals with respect to access to information and can greater a denial of rights and services.

On June 26, Russian media spread a statement by the chief of the Foreign Intelligence Service of Russia, Sergei Naryshkin, that Ukraine planned to export valuables, including the relics of saints, from the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra to France, Germany, Italy, and the Vatican. Allegedly, the return of the relics to Ukraine “is not planned.”

On the evening of June 27, the Russians launched a missile attack on the Ria Lounge pizzeria in the centre of Kramatorsk, Donetsk Oblast. As a result of the strike, 12 people were killed, 65 were injured.
Russian propagandists traditionally accused the Ukrainian Armed Forces of the attack.

But later, the official version was “a high-precision strike on the temporary deployment point of the 56th Separate Motorized Infantry Brigade of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.”

After the death of Italian politician and businessman Silvio Berlusconi, pro-Russian resources promoted an outright fake about Ukraine’s claims to his inheritance. The messages were based on a completely fictional statement by the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine Dmytro Kuleba. He allegedly said that Berlusconi was a friend of Putin, and therefore Europe should confiscate all the property of the deceased and give it to Ukraine as compensation for the war crimes of Russia.

subindicator: ILS2.2 - Accessible, safe and accurate information
justification: Information about aid in Somalia is becoming more available but not to everyone.

Amnesty International has criticized Zimbabwe's authorities for not providing a progress report on the investigation into journalist and pro-democracy activist Itai Dzamara's disappearance eight years ago. The organization believes the lack of action in ensuring justice and truth for Dzamara's family sends a chilling message about the security of others demanding accountability from the government.

Two years ago this Thursday (April 7), Mozambican journalist Ibraimo Mbaruco went missing in Cabo Delgado.

Mbaruco was kidnapped while on his way home from work at Rádio Comunitário de Palma at around 7:00 p.m. on April 7, 2020. The journalist managed to tell colleagues via text message that he was “surrounded by soldiers”, but since then, the authorities have said nothing about his whereabouts.

The Ethiopian Human Rights Commission denounced the arrest and detention of journalists in a statement as ‘’unlawful’’, noting that the country’s media law prohibits pre-trial detention for any alleged offenses committed through the media, and called for the immediate release of the journalists.

The Ministry of Information and Media's Permanent Secretary, Kennedy Kalunga, addressed misinformation surrounding the 2023 Financial Intelligence Centre (FIC) Annual Report. The report focuses on activities undertaken by the FIC during the 2022 financial year, analyzing 155 cases worth K6.1 billion. The report includes cases carried over from previous years, emphasizing the need to account for prior investigations. The government aims to provide clarity and dispel misconceptions about the report's contents.

The Zambian government has issued a warning against fake news, urging individuals to avoid spreading false information. Thabo Kawana, Director Spokesperson in the Ministry of Information and Media, emphasized the importance of creating and publicizing forged documents. Kawana stated that fabricating and presenting forged documents as authentic violates Section 344 of the penal code, Chapter 87 of Zambia's laws.

The last journalist known to have disappeared in Cabo Delgado was Ibrahimo Mbaruco, in April 2020. He went missing after meeting a group of government soldiers in Palma town and has not been heard from since. The Mozambican government has not publicly disclosed the status of the investigations, if any, into his disappearance.

The government has identified fake documents on social media claiming to be written by President HakAINDE HICHILEMA and Home Affairs Permanent Secretary Josephs Akafumbab. The letters are titled "CONTAIN the Catholic Church in Zambia." Information and Media Director Spokesperson THABO KAWANA is concerned about the publication of false information and warns all online administrators to be prosecuted for alarming the nation.

Mwangala Zaloumis, Chairperson of the Electoral Commission of Zambia, argues that misinformation during polls poses a threat to credible elections. She aims to prevent electoral violence from reoccurring, as it would put the Commission in a difficult position. Zaloumis believes that the ECZ has been a victim of misinformation, disinformation, media play, and social media as threats to a credible election.

Zambia's low digital literacy and skills levels, at around 35%, have exposed the country to cybercrime, according to Technology and Science Minister Felix Mutati. This leaves the country globally unprotected and calls for urgent acceleration of digital literacy and skills to realize Zambia's smart program agenda.

Zambia experienced a 45% increase in international investments in the first six months of 2022, according to Minister of Technology and Science Felix Mutati. The country is now using Microsoft's Azure Stack platform to support investors. Smart Zambia Institute is training over 3,200 teachers in Digital Literacy, and laptops with Intel Core processors are available to teachers through civil service loan agreements.

Smart Zambia and NETONE have signed a Memorandum of Understanding to train 10,000 teachers in digital literacy. The program will begin on May 1st and be completed within 12 months. The collaboration aims to create affordable access to digital devices and enhance education delivery using Information Communication Technology Platforms, in line with the 8th National Development Plan.

Zambia's Technology and Science Minister FELIX MUTATI reveals that the government has implemented strategies to increase digital literacy, which currently stands at 34% in the country. This is low compared to other African countries with over 50% literacy levels. Zambia's President HAKAINDE HICHILEMA is a champion for technology transformation, and United Nations Assistant Secretary General Fayaza King has praised the country's efforts in enhancing technology in its education sector.

The House of Peoples' Representatives approved the New Media Law on February 2, 2021, bringing hope for a better repressive environment. Under the EPRDF, journalists and media personnel faced human rights violations like torture, arrest, detention, and intimidation. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed pledged to transition the country into a democracy by opening political space and ensuring freedom of expression in 2018.

MTN Group has launched the MTN Skills Academy in Zambia, a free online learning platform aimed at closing the digital skills gap in Africa. The pan-African telecom aims to develop sustainable digital skills in at least 60% of young people in 19 markets by 2025, aligning with the African Union's digital transformation agenda.

Ethiopia aims to achieve 70% digital literacy and financial inclusion by 2025, emphasizing digital and financial literacy. MInT, the government's digital agency, emphasizes interventions like EdTech cultivation, prioritizing basic literacy and digital skills, and collaborating with strategic partners to address literacy gaps.

Ethio telecom aims to digitalize daily business activities and improve customer service experiences. They have signed a strategic partnership with Tecno Mobile Limited and Transsion Manufacturing PLC to purchase and sell Techno's CAMON 20 commercial mobile series. This collaboration will ensure consistent supply of Techno devices, enhance joint channel development, and increase smartphone penetration, bridging the digital divide in Ethiopia.

The Honduran journalist and former candidate for deputy in her country, Kenia Lili González Sánchez, was expelled from Nicaragua on Friday, August 4, 2023 for 'defending' the persecuted Catholic priests in Nicaragua, denounced the victim in a video published on her social networks. At the border post, they read her a document in which they informed her "she was a person not well received by the Government of Nicaragua for making publications in favor of Christians in Nicaragua.

Nelson Matus, the director of Lo Real de Guerrero (a popular digital news outlet specializing in crime news and citizens complaints in Acapulco and its surroundings) was killed in the port of Acapulco on July 15. Armed men approached him and fired several shots.
Seven communicators have been murdered in Mexico so far in 2023 and two have been murdered in Acapulco in less than three months.

The magazine Txoro Matutino, of Cuernavaca, Morelos, was attacked on Saturday night [Aug. 5] and early Sunday morning [Aug. 6] with at least five gunshots, with no injuries reported, informed Juan José Arrese, general director of the magazine. According to the version of the director of Txoro Matutino, when they arrived to broadcast their morning edition this Monday, Aug. 7, they noticed there were at least five gunshots in the front of their facilities.

The Inter American Press Association (IAPA) condemned another attack by the Nicaraguan regime against journalism, after learning of the banishment of journalist Marcos Medina, who were prevented from entering the country. Medina, director of the digital news outlet Fuentes Confiables [Trustworthy sources], was visiting United States, on a family medical matter. On July 24, when he was about to return to his country with his wife and daughter, the airline notified them that the Nicaraguan Directorate of Immigration and Alien Affairs had denied them entry into the country.

Ticay was arrested on Thursday, April 6, 2023, after he filmed and gave coverage to the Catholic tradition known as La Reseña, during the Holy Week festivities. The activity was being held despite orders from Vice President Rosario Murillo ordering all Catholic processions banned that week. Since April 6, Ticay had been held in the District III police station in Managua.

The Inter-American Press Association (IAPA) condemned the intensification of 'repression' by the Daniel Ortega regime against the media in Nicaragua on Thursday [May 11]. The regime's actions have resulted in the detention of three journalists since last April in the Central American country. In a statement, the organization, based in Miami, urged the international community to denounce the regime's persecution of freedom of expression and the press.

During the campaign, Costa Rican media reported serious allegations against the elected President, including suspicions of sexual harassment and illegal campaign financing. In response to this, the then-candidate began a systematic persecution of some news outlets, with frequent verbal attacks. Three news outlets that are audience leaders in their respective sectors are at the center of the attacks: daily newspaper La Nación, TV station Canal 7, and news portal CRHoy.com. Chaves has already used terms against them such as "scumbag press" and "political assassins.”

subindicator: ILS4.4 - Deliberate communication shutdowns / restrictions from malicious actors
justification: The Inter American Press Association (IAPA) denounced the continued abuse of defamation lawsuits against Panamanian media and journalists and the preventive seizure of their assets as mechanisms of intimidation and gagging to curb critical journalism

subindicator: ILS4.4 - Deliberate communication shutdowns / restrictions from malicious actors
justification: In Africa, Internet users in Ethiopia have been the hardest hit by Internet disruptions, with popular social media and messaging services (TikTok, Facebook, Telegram, YouTube) being blocked nationally since 9 February amid religious tensions and calls for anti-government protests. At a regional level, many of the six million people living in Ethiopia’s Tigray region continue to live through the longest-running Internet shutdown, now well over 960 days long.

subindicator: ILS4.4 - Deliberate communication shutdowns / restrictions from malicious actors
justification:
In 2022, Ethiopia lost $179.9 million to 8,760 hours of internet shutdown, causing a blackout for 1,767,500 internet users. In the same year, Nigeria lost $82.7 million to 287 hours of social media shutdown for 104,400,000 users.
“The most severe internet outages in 2023 to date have been in Ethiopia, where authorities blocked access to Facebook and YouTube following an escalation of religious tensions in early February.

A service run by the Open Observatory of Network Interference (OONI), an association that tracks online censorship, showed that access to social networks in Africa’s second-most populous country was freely available after being shut down in early February.

An AFP journalist in Addis Ababa was able to access sites including Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok without using a virtual private network (VPN), a mechanism that enables an internet connection from a different location.

On the 7th of September 2022, the founder and editor of the Voice of Amhara was arrested by authorities at his home. He was accused of having ties with the TLPF and attempting to terrorise the public by disseminating information that supports the rebel group. No formal charges were laid against him.

Freedom of expression has been restricted, with journalists and media actors facing detentions, arrests, and censorship. On September 7, 2022, the founder and editor of the Voice of Amhara was arrested for alleged ties to the TLPF and attempting to terrorize the public. No formal charges were laid against him.

Ethiopia's human rights situation has been severely impacted by extrajudicial killings, rape, sexual violence, unlawful shelling, airstrikes, and pillage over the past two years. Freedom of expression has been restricted, with journalists and media actors facing detentions, arrests, and censorship. On September 7, 2022, the founder and editor of the Voice of Amhara was arrested for alleged ties to the TLPF and attempting to terrorize the public. No formal charges were laid against him.

Journalists were allowed more time for investigation and were arrested. “It is unacceptable by any measure,” the Ethiopian Media Council criticized the charges brought against journalists who were arrested in connection with their work. The council asked to look into the judicial system “only through media proclamations”. Arrested journalists were allowed to be detained “like any other defendant” and the council criticized this as “unacceptable by any measure”. The council mentioned regarding the recent arrests of journalists

Amhara journalists Genet Asmamaw and Meskerem Abera taken by police. The Coalition For Women In Journalism is alarmed by the treatment and targeting of Amhara journalists. We demand their immediate and unconditional release.

The human rights commission urges the government to stop arbitrary arrests of journalists and respect citizens' rights. They also urge lifting internet restrictions on social media, as they violate human rights. The call was made during the Ethiopian Media Council's celebration of world press freedom day on May 3, 2023, with journalists present.

The Ethiopian Human Rights Commission and the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) have condemned a wave of journalist arrests, including eight who support the Amhara ethnic group. The arrests occurred between April 3 and 13, mainly in Addis Ababa. The CPJ stated that these journalists were arrested for their support of the Amhara group.

The Ethiopian Human Rights Commission and the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) have condemned a wave of journalist arrests, including eight who support the Amhara ethnic group. The arrests occurred between April 3-13, mainly in Addis Ababa. The CPJ stated that these journalists are sympathetic to the Amhara's cause.

Last June, derived from the serious situation that freedom of expression is experiencing in Guatemala, the Red Rompe el Miedo Guatemala carried out an electoral monitoring of the attacks that occurred against journalists and communicators during the first round of the elections. The Network reported a total of 27 incidents that affected a total of 38 journalists and communicators. Obstructing journalistic work was reported among the most recurrent attacks, as well as specific cases of intimidation in silenced areas.

The indigenous and community journalists interviewed by the mission remarked that have faced and resisted violence of the State in their territories in a continuous and sustained manner. It is so at least since the end of the internal armed conflict, especially in areas where local authorities historically have colluded with powers that be, such as transnational corporations and organized crime groups, to silence the voices of those who oppose the dispossession of their lands and natural resources.

subindicator: ILS2.2 - Accessible, safe and accurate information
justification: UNHCR response report in venezuela during the period of January to June 2023 hilights that the response focused in communication with communities: Information Rehabilitation to institutions and community and prioritized communities Individual  attention: Orientation, sessions and broadcasting of key messages through media and messaging apps legal assistance and psycho-social.

Journalists from Colón reported to the Committee for Free Expression that on several occasions they have had information deleted from their news outlets, after calls or messages warned them about certain people's discomfort with news they broadcast. According to the version of journalists whose names are withheld for security reasons, the last incident was reported this week [July 3] when the director of a digital news outlet was asked by phone by two different people to remove a story about insecurity in a sector of Tocoa.

In the last ten days, at least four journalists in Tegucigalpa and San Pedro Sula have received death threats through platforms and social media. The increase in threats and intimidation against journalists and media outlets is produced by unknown persons who have said to be against the opinions issued and the work of these communicators.

Haitian journalist, Blondine Tanis, was released on Sunday night [July 30], following the payment of a ransom to the individuals who kidnapped her. After her release, Tanis was taken to a hospital. She was beaten by her captors to force her relatives to pay, according to local media. The co-host of the program "Tribune Matinale [Morning tribune]" belonging to Radio Rénovation FM, was kidnapped when she was entering her house in the neighborhood of Delmas, in Port-au-Prince (capital of Haiti), last July 21.

Around 6 a.m. on Sunday, July 23, about 50 heavily armed men with assault-style rifles attacked the town of Liancourt in Haiti’s Artibonite region, burning down dozens of houses and the Radio Antarctique studio, according to videos reviewed by CPJ and the station’s director and founder Roderson Elias, who spoke with CPJ in a phone interview.

On June 13, Marie Lucie Bonhomme, a journalist with Radio Vision 2000 and owner of the radio and television station Télé Pluriel, was forcibly taken from her residence and released hours later. Four other journalists were kidnapped and released after their ransoms were paid this year: Robert Dénis, general director of TV Canal Bleu; Lebrun Saint-Hubert, president and general director of community radio 2000; Jean Thony Lorthé, host of the program 'Rafrechi Memwa' on Radio Vision 2000; and Sandra Duvivier, cultural journalist, cameraman and staff member of Telemax.

Palestinians are constantly monitored in public places. Their private spaces are often intruded without their knowledge, through monitoring of online platforms like Facebook, calls, and online conversations considered "threatening," and tracking the location and connections of mobile phones. Colonies are equipped with technologies that enhance identification, arrest, and detention of Palestinians engaging in protests or resisting the expansion of colonies. In addition to extensive control, the occupation has advanced Israel’s development surveillance technologies, including facial recognition, and social media monitoring.

A well-known Haitian journalist was kidnapped from her home and hours later was freed by one of the dangerous gangs operating in Port-au-Prince. Marie Lucie Bonhomme Opont, a journalist for Radio Vision 2000, was kidnapped at 3:00 a.m. on June 13 at her residence in the Tabarre neighborhood, northeast of the Haitian capital, by the gang known as 'Kraze Baryè' led by Vitelhomme Innocent, a fugitive from justice, according to the victim.

Another journalist was murdered within 48 hours in Haiti, the most dangerous country in which to practice journalism, according to a preliminary report by the Inter American Press Association (IAPA) released Tuesday [April 25]. The body of Ricot Jean, a journalist with Radio-Télé Évolution Inter in Saint-Marc, a town 73 km [45 miles] north of Port-au-Prince, was found in an open field on Tuesday morning [April 25], according to Alcide Volcy, the station's information director, quoted by the newspaper Le Nouvelliste.

Jorge Ugalde, a journalist in Quintana Roo, was the victim of a gun attack on Sunday, July 30, when his home, located in the municipality of Benito Juárez, was shot at. Through a video, Ugalde denounced the attack against him and shared evidence, in which it can be seen that at least two individuals were responsible for the aggression. The attack against the journalist took place around 8:00 pm on Sunday, when the two individuals approached his home and shot at it. Ugalde explained that fortunately, at that moment, he was not at home.

The Prosecutor of Nayarit, Petronilo Díaz Ponce Medrano, confirmed to La Jornada newspaper that journalist Osiris Maldonado de la Paz, who was kidnapped on July 3, was found alive. Maldonado de la Paz was abducted in recent days, as also was Jonathan Lora Ramírez, who was last seen in the community of El Armadillo on July 7, and who was also released by his captors yesterday. This is related to the kidnapping and murder of Luis Martín Sánchez Íñiguez, a news correspondent for La Jornada, who was abducted on July 5 and whose remains were found yesterday in a rural town called Ahuacate. According to the first investigations, the abduction of the three press members is likely to be related to their journalism, and it is believed they worked together at some point in their professional careers.

subindicator: ILS4.4 - Deliberate communication shutdowns / restrictions from malicious actors
justification: The Ethiopian Human Rights Commission reported civilian attacks, property damage, and transportation and internet services suspensions in Amhara. Ethiopian Airlines has suspended flights to Dessie, Lalibela, and Gondar. Tensions in the region have grown since the government announced plans to dismantle special forces, which Amhara nationalists protested as a threat to their region.

subindicator: ILS2.1 - Telecommunications infrastructures damage or limitations
justification: Ethiopia has one of the highest road traffic fatality rates globally due to weak driver regulation, poor vehicle condition, and poorly maintained road networks. Despite investments in power, the electricity supply remains inadequate, with frequent outages in towns and cities. Internet access is limited in urban centers and hindered by slow speeds, connectivity issues, and government censorship.

On July 29th, journalist Jose Rubén Zamora marks a year in detention in Guatemala. He faced legal harassment and was unjustly sentenced to six years in prison on false charges in June 2023.

The unjust imprisonment and conviction of José Rubén Zamora, a Guatemalan publisher, on false money-laundering charges are tactics employed by the government to suppress independent journalism. A government attacking press freedom puts all other liberties at risk.
Guatemalan journalists faced heightened attacks since President Jimmy Morales assumed office in 2016. The country now ranks 127th out of 180 in RSF’s Press Freedom Index.

Guatemalan journalists face rising hostility and violence, especially those investigating political corruption. Reporters and media outlets in the country endure frequent harassment and intimidation, creating a challenging environment for free press.

During the last year, President Alejandro Giammattei's government has intensified efforts to criminalize journalism in Guatemala. A distressing episode was the unjust imprisonment and sentencing of investigative journalist José Rubén Zamora. This reflects a wider crackdown aiming to stifle those challenging corruption. Zamora's lawyers were intimidated, his newspaper closed, and over 20 local journalists fled seeking safety.

Giammattei's government, along with Attorney General Consuelo Porras, have fostered a hostile atmosphere for free journalism in Guatemala. This includes verbal assaults, press restrictions, and oppressive legal actions, collectively amounting to censorship of independent journalists and media entities.

The Giammattei administration and Attorney General Consuelo Porras have jeopardized the safety of independent journalists and media outlets. Their actions include verbal attacks, press restrictions, and abusive criminal proceedings, undermining the safety and well-being of journalists in Guatemala.

During the initial half of 2022, Guatemala's Journalists’ Association documented 66 cases of attacks, persecution, and criminalization against media professionals. Government authorities have misused a 2008 anti-gender-based violence law, alleging 'psychological violence' to target journalists who report on them, particularly when the reporting involves government officials or their female family members.

On March 8, Orlando Villanueva, a journalist with Noticias del Puerto, was fatally shot by unidentified assailants in Puerto Barrios, Izabal's capital. Journalists in the same department have endured assaults and government harassment, especially when reporting on a mining venture in the Indigenous El Estor community.

In September, journalist Carlos Choc from Prensa Comunitaria was acquitted by a judge. Unfounded charges of 'incitement to commit crime' were leveled against him due to his coverage of an October 2021 protest linked to a mining project.

In April, journalist Juan Luis Font fled Guatemala due to unjust criminal investigations tied to his reporting on corruption involving ex-infrastructure minister Alejandro Sinibaldi. Sinibaldi, currently under investigation for bribery, faced Font's exposés on corruption allegations.

In July, authorities detained José Rubén Zamora, the owner of reputable media outlet El Periódico, known for exposing corruption in Guatemala. Zamora faces allegations of 'money laundering,' 'blackmail,' and 'influence peddling.

On August 11, unknown assailants fatally shot two journalists while they were traveling on a motorcycle in Caballo Blanco town, located in the southwestern Retalhuleu department. Various news reports confirm this tragic event.

Since 1992, at least six journalists have been murdered in Guatemala due to their journalistic endeavors, as revealed by CPJ's research. Journalists face threats and intimidation, stemming from both organized crime and government figures. Investigative journalist José Rubén Zamora is currently serving a six-year prison sentence for his work, a case closely monitored by CPJ.

When acclaimed Guatemalan journalist José Rubén Zamora was apprehended at his residence in July the prior year, both local and international organizations demanded his prompt release, citing apprehensions over press freedom.

The Association of Journalists of Guatemala (APG) recorded almost 400 instances of harassment and limitations imposed on journalists throughout President Alejandro Giammattei's current term. These include legal measures used to silence, criminalize, and impede reporters' work.

Award-winning Guatemalan journalist José Rubén Zamora, aged 66 and founder of a prominent newspaper, received a six-year prison sentence for money laundering. Human rights observers view this conviction as a grave threat to press freedom and democracy within Guatemala, marking a concerning development.

On Wednesday, a Guatemalan court sentenced prominent journalist Jose Zamora to a six-year prison term for money laundering. Zamora, known for critical reporting on successive governments, denounces the case as political persecution by President Alejandro Giammattei. Rights groups view it as an assault on free speech, citing Zamora's reporting on alleged corruption involving the president and his allies in the now-defunct elPeriodico newspaper.

In Guatemala, journalists and communicators face harassment and criminalization, both offline and online, aiming to suppress their voices and curtail freedom of expression. The state's failure to ensure a violence-free environment for defending human rights has adversely affected civil society. Additionally, powerful groups exert significant influence, particularly over the justice system, impacting the impartiality of judicial decisions.

Journalist safety is a longstanding concern in Guatemala, particularly within areas where community media operate amidst collaboration between organized crime, public officials, and national or international corporations, aiming to stifle journalistic inquiries. The press is perceived as a threat to vested interests, leading to increasing harassment and criminalization of journalists, constituting a modern form of censorship.

Official state advertising misuse and pressure on advertisers contribute to media suppression. Coordinated cyber-attacks, like those by the Fundación Contra el Terrorismo, lead to persistent digital harassment, fostering a climate of fear and prompting journalists to engage in self-censorship.

Facing threats and criminal charges for exposing influential figures, over 20 journalists have fled Guatemala. Remaining journalists live under surveillance and constant fear, enduring death threats, occasionally from political candidates, highlighting significant concerns regarding journalist safety in the country.

Zimbabweans are being trained to spot fake news on social media, which experts believe threatens to undermine democracy and fuel political-motivated violence. The training is being conducted as the southern African nation prepares for elections next year, with incidents such as an opposition leader quitting, voting postponement for rural residents, and a man being eaten by a lion.

Zimbabweans formed social media groups to support their political parties and candidates during the 23 August election. Some formed joint ruling and opposition party information sharing groups, mostly on WhatsApp, debating politics and promoting their views. These groups displayed the underbelly of social media, including hate messaging threats, misinformation, and disinformation.

Zimbabwe's upcoming elections on 23 August face growing government censorship, with a history of internet shutdowns dating back to 2019. Denying access to the internet and communication platforms could disrupt and delegitimize the 2023 elections, as millions of people will be heading to the polls. Access to the internet is essential before, during, and after the elections.

Reporters Without Borders (RSF) is calling on Zimbabwean authorities to prevent journalists from being obstructed during the upcoming general elections and not arbitrarily suspend the internet or social media. In April, five journalists were denied accreditation to cover the First Lady's visit to the Museum of African Liberation in Harare, with security personnel stating that only state media could access the museum.

On 17 July, ruling Zanu PF party members attacked Annahstacia Ndlovu, a reporter for Voice of America Zimbabwe television, during scuffles in Bulawayo, causing her to sustain an abdominal injury and delete her videos.

With 52.6% of the vote, Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa was reelected, avoiding a runoff against opposition leader Nelson Chamisa. Rejecting the outcome, the opposition described the vote as "fraught with unprecedented illegality." Censored media coverage and new legislation such as the Patriotic Bill were given as justifications for the arrest of more than forty local poll observers. The opposition called the findings "criminal" and "doctored."

Such centers violate the right to liberty and a fair trial. Also, no information is made public.

There are approximately 200 Afghan journalists at risk in Pakistan according to the Pakistan-Afghan International Forum of Journalists. Asad* an Afghan journalist hiding in Pakistan said: “Even though I entered Pakistan on a valid visa and have applied for renewal, I do not have anything to show the authorities if they turn up at my doorstep.'

A veteran investigative reporter has been arrested under Türkiye’s “disinformation” law for referring in an article to judicial corruption cases cited by the Istanbul public prosecutor.

Türkiye’s “disinformation” law has been used since taking effect a year ago. government hast used this as a tool for persecuting journalists, especially investigative reporters and those covering the aftermath of the earthquake in February.  It has helped to reinforce the climate of intimidation for journalists, who are already subject to many other forms of judicial harassment.

They were subjected to months of judicial pressure and attempts to discredit their reporting. This is liable to encourage self-censorship, and therefore constitutes a violation of the freedom of expression that is guaranteed by the European Convention on Human Rights, as the Council of Europe and Venice Commission pointed out in a joint “urgent opinion” issued on 7 October 2022.

More than 200 Afghan journalists are threatened with deportation from Pakistan, as it's ordered undocumented Afghan citizens to leave by 1 November.  RSF has interviewed several of them, and they report an increase in violence against them since the government issued its expulsion threat. They have been subjected to harassment and extortion by Pakistani police officers, arbitrary arrest, pressure on landlords to expel Afghan tenants and never-ending visa application procedures.

Majid Hyderi’s detention has brought the number of journalists currently held in Jammu and Kashmir to six. Majid is a freelance journalist who has been held arbitrarily for more than three weeks. he has also been very critical of corruption within the Kashmiri bureaucracy and New Delhi’s failure to address this problem also known for his moderate political views and criticizing attacks against the security forces in, both the local police and the army.

When they contacted their Internet service provider, they were told that the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology had quite simply blocked access to their site under the 2000 Information Technology Act.

subindicator: ILS4.4 - Deliberate communication shutdowns / restrictions from malicious actors

Repeated Internet shutdowns for years in Jammu and Kashmir have transformed the region into a news and information black hole.

The amendment that the Indian government adopted in disinformation allows it, to order Internet access providers and “social media intermediaries to take down any content which, in its view, provides “fake, false or misleading” information. government took complete control over established print media and TV news channels, the Internet is the only way remaining for citizens to be informed. So, the government has brought in legislation to control of the Internet and social media platforms

Mortaza Behboudi, Arrested by a Taliban intelligence agency in the Afghan capital, Kabul, on 7 January and held for a total of 284 days, on charges of spying, illegal support for foreigners, and assisting border crossings. His release was the culmination of a campaign in his defense that RSF had waged. he was arrested outside Kabul University while interviewing women who were banned from studying. He was accused of spying, He was repeatedly interrogated during the months.

subindicator: ILS2.2 - Accessible, safe and accurate information
justification: The regime has allowed the widespread adoption of mobile phones, including smartphones, but has developed technical measures that allow it to completely control communications within the country’s intranet. North Koreans can still be sent to a concentration camp to look at an online media outlet based outside the country.

As a result of the regime’s desire for complete isolation from the world, journalists have been arrested, deported, sent to forced labour camps, and killed for deviating from the party’s narrative. In 2017, the government even sentenced South Korean journalists to death in absentia for only commenting on the country’s economic and social situation.

What with the risks of arrest, abduction, torture or murder, Syrian journalists are often forced to flee the country to escape mistreatment or death. Several who had found refuge in Turkey were forced to return in 2019. Hundreds of others were threatened with the same fate, which would have exposed them to arrest by the Syrian authorities or to abuses at the hands of various armed groups if the Turkish authorities had not finally given up on this measure.

Ethiopia's four-month social media ban has severely impacted communications businesses and civil rights groups, making it difficult for them to reach audiences and verify information. The ban, imposed in March, was triggered by a disagreement with the Orthodox Church, leading to protests.

Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has cracked down on media outlets and journalists, including detaining journalists and intimidating prominent online reporters.

Over the last decade, Russia has utilized and honed a variety of information warfare methods. The Russian government has been credibly implicated in hacking attacks on the websites and e-mail addresses of major media agencies and government officials to plant and send fake information. It has also been credibly implicated in using deep fakes, creating websites based on fake identities or institutions to share false or misleading information, and using trolls and bots to spread and lend credibility to disinformation.

The ICT, Postal and Courier Services ministry has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the Computer Society of Zimbabwe (CSZ) to expedite civil servants' digital literacy certification. The MoU was signed during the CSZ 2023 summit, aiming to ensure all civil servants are certified in the International Computer Driving Licence (ICDL), a crucial skill for Zimbabwe's digital literacy.

During the Girls in ICT Day event at the Transform Africa Summit in Zimbabwe, H.E. Dr. Amani Abou-Zeid, African Union Commissioner for Infrastructure and Energy, underlined the need for more powerful women to engage in the fourth industrial revolution. 'Digital Skills for Life' is the day's topic, and speakers talked on how to improve digital skills through mentoring, education, and getting more kids involved.

Mozambique's digital transformation poses new threats to end-users, including the government and private sector. Public entities face risks from online information storage, leading the government to prioritize cybersecurity as a key segment in the country's digital transformation process.

According to the materials of the Security Service of Ukraine and the State Bureau of Investigation the people's Deputy Dubinskiy was charged with treason: 
he was part of a criminal organization formed by General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces: their main task was shaking the socio-political situation in Ukraine and discrediting the state in the international arena. Members of group received money from Russian military intelligence. The suspect was spreading fakes about higher military and political leadership of Ukraine.

According to a British Ministry of Defense, Russian authorities are actively using history as a tool to sow anti-Western sentiment among their citizens and intimidate their neighbors. Particular attention is paid to the compilation of a collection of documents entitled "On the historical unity of Russians and Ukrainians" which includes an article by the Russian dictator Putin and his address on situation in Ukraine. The collection contains 242 documents from different periods and is used to justify Kremlin's policy.

Last week, Chad's media regulator, the High Media and Audiovisual Authority (HAMA), suspended Alwihda Info for eight days following its publication of articles on an internal reshuffle within the army and on a speech given by the transitional president, Mahamat Déby, about the conflict raging in the north of the country, near the Libyan border.

The Media Council of Tanzania reported that in 2020, the number of journalists being censured for their work in Tanzania decreased slightly, with 17 reported violations, including threats, arrests, denial of access to information, and equipment seizures, compared to 25 in 2021 and 41 in 2020. This decrease in press freedom raises hopes for improvement in the country.

Journalists Fortune Francis and Sunday George were assaulted and their phones stolen while covering a political rally in Dar es Salaam. They were working for Mwananchi Communications Limited, which publishes Mwananchi and Mwanaspoti newspapers. The International Federation of Journalists (IFJ) and the Journalists Workers’ Union of Tanzania (JOWUTA) condemn the incident.

The Centre of Competence in Digital Education (C-CoDE) is a $100,000 facility in Tanzania and the East Africa Community that aims to transform training and educational practices using digital tools and technologies. It features a professional studio for live streaming and recording educational content.

Tanzania is set to become a digital hub within the East Africa Community (EAC) with the launch of the Centre of Competence in Digital Education (C-CoDE), hosted by the Nelson Mandela African Institution of Science and Technology (NM-AIST) under the Excellence in Africa initiative, a collaboration between Morocco's Mohamed VI Polytechnic University and Switzerland's Ecole Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne.

Tanzania, an East African country, has implemented the Data Use Partnership (DUP) to revolutionize its healthcare system by integrating a people-centered approach and utilizing comprehensive health information, demonstrating the transformative potential of digital health in the global healthcare landscape.

The World Bank's recent report indicates that Tanzanian youth are only 1.7% employed in the digital economy, compared to 3.2% in Kenya and 5.6% in Nigeria. This disparity is attributed to the country's weak digital infrastructure, limited digital skills training, and lack of awareness of digital job opportunities among Tanzanian youth.

In March 2022, the Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority and Cenerva facilitated a Digital Economy Training Program for Tanzania High-Level Policy Makers in Zanzibar, aiming to create a comprehensive understanding of the Digital Economy for Tanzania's future economic growth.

The Tanzanian government plans to invest USD 4.7 billion to train 500 state civil servants in information and communication technologies (ICT) to help populations adopt digital services. The initiative was unveiled by Mohammed Khamis Abdulla, permanent secretary of the Ministry of Information, Communication and Information Technology. Digital technology is a key pillar of the country's socio-economic development.

Tanzania's rapid digital literacy rate is boosting business success and economic growth. With increased internet access, businesses can reach new customers, improve operations, and increase productivity, resulting in increased economic activity and job creation across the country.

Orkeeswa is partnering with Team4Tech to enhance its impact on dozens of schools and over 20,000 students and teachers by increasing its technological capacity through skills training, hardware, and software. Team4Tech will support this by promoting computer literacy, a robotics curriculum, and increasing access to computers, tablets, and projectors.

Professor Anicia Peters, Chief Executive Officer of the National Commission of Research Science and Technology, highlighted the issue of digital literacy in Namibia despite the growing opportunities in Artificial Intelligence. She spoke at Youth Quake Namibia's annual event, which aimed to promote digital rights among the youth and empower them in the digital era.

Namibia's Ministry of Information and Communication Technology (MICT) has requested the AU-EU D4D Hub's support to enhance digital literacy in the country. The goal is to achieve 100% digital literacy by 2030, but challenges persist in reaching rural communities and the adult and elderly population, despite the MICT's progress in achieving this goal.

The Ministry of Information and Communication Technology has awarded certificates to youth participants from Kalkveld, Omaruru, Katima Mulilo, and Okatyali for their participation in the two-week Digital Literacy training programme, aiming to expand digital literacy programs in the country.

Namibia's President Hage Gottfried Geingob highlighted the potential of the digital revolution and emerging technologies in his UN General Assembly 2023 address. He stressed the need to prevent developing countries from being left behind in this transformation. Geingob emphasized the importance of technology transfer, adoption, skill development, and collaboration in bridging gaps in education, healthcare, and economic development.

On 5th September 2023, over 80 professionals from government, academia, civil society, and the private sector convened in Windhoek to discuss the implementation of UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, organized by the Ministry of Higher Education, Training, and Innovation in collaboration with UNESCO.

The Zambezi region's information ministry, backed by the AU-EU Digital Hub, recently launched a two-day digital literacy program, training around 50 people to enhance digital literacy in rural areas, aiming to improve the region's digital literacy.

Professor Anicia Peters of the National Commission of Research Science and Technology (NCRST) warns that digital literacy in Namibia is a concern despite the growing opportunities in Artificial Intelligence, with the World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2023 predicting 69 million new jobs by 2027.

At the ninth annual session of DRIF, stakeholders in Namibia discussed internet rights issues. The deputy minister of information and communication technology, Emma Theofilus, announced a collaboration with the Digital Foundation of Namibia to tackle low literacy levels in ICT.

Namibia is facing a surge in cybersecurity risks, including phishing, malware, and data breaches, as businesses and individuals increasingly rely on technology. In 2022, the country experienced a 40% increase in reported cyberattacks, highlighting the need for awareness and mitigation measures, as highlighted by Kamal Tour, UNODC's acting head of cybercrime programmes in Africa.

Speaking at the opening of the 7th National Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Summit in Windhoek, the capital of Namibia, on Monday, Minister of Information and Communication Technology Peya Mushelenga said there is a need to ensure protection for application security, network security, and data security, among others.

Namibia's rapid digitization and technological advancements necessitate robust cybersecurity measures, as sophisticated threats like phishing attacks, ransomware, and data breaches pose significant risks to individuals, businesses, and government institutions.

Namibia has established a cyber security council that would act as a useful forum for discussions and developing operational strategies to tackle cybercrime in banking and non-bank financial institutions.

According to the second Deputy Governor of the Bank of Namibia, Leonie Dunn, the council would ensure that the issues around cyber security within the sector are given the priority they actually deserve.

International Fact-Checking Day 2023, observed on 2 April, highlights media and technology issues. Namibia Fact Check has observed a surge in online scams, WhatsApp as a primary channel for spreading misinformation, and Covid-19-related disinformation and conspiracy theories, particularly around vaccines. These phenomena underscore the need for a deeper understanding of the media landscape's role in shaping public perception.

This has caused misinformation to proliferate and facts to be twisted, which could have detrimental effects on society.

The 2018/19 – 2020/21 National Education and Training Sector Improvement Program aims to increase the number of schools with computers, computer laboratories, and science laboratories, ensuring the introduction of ICT in the education sector.

The Central Bank of Eswatini (CBCE) is exploring the idea of issuing a Digital Lilangeni as a complement to cash, focusing on governance, accessibility, interoperability, security, and programmability aspects to ensure consumers continue access to legally backed central bank money.

Scammers hacked into EswatiniBank systems, transferring approximately E140 million into various accounts. Hacking involves gaining unauthorised access to data, and the money was then transferred to ATMs across the country, causing widespread withdrawals.

The Foreign Affairs Minister has accused editor Zweli Martin Dlamini and Swaziland News of spreading disinformation about Eswatini. The Minister has stated that efforts are being made to correct the deliberate misinformation that is fueling the campaign to unsettle the country. The report calls for greater engagement with diplomatic communities to counter the misguided narrative that has spread through mainstream media.

Press freedom is under threat as new laws restricting journalists' work and freedom of expression are debated in the national parliament. Public hearings are ongoing on proposed drafts of a new media and broadcasting law, which local and international groups argue would criminalize journalists' work.

The draft law prohibits the rebroadcasting of foreign political shows, restricts the number of correspondents from international broadcasters and media outlets to two per outlet, and restricts journalists' right to defend themselves in defamation cases against the president. Parliament has not scheduled a final debate and approval date.

As of 12 October 2023, since fighting started in mid-April between the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces, partly due to tensions over the Sudanese army’s attempted integration of the RSF, many journalists covering the fighting have been shot, beaten, and harassed. Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ)’s emails to the Sudanese Armed Forces and the RSF received no replies.

On 10 October 2023, soldiers from Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary group killed Halima Idris Salim when they ran over the journalist with a vehicle.

Salim, a reporter for local independent online news outlet Sudan Bukra, was covering the conflict in the city of Omdurman, northwest of the capital of Khartoum.

As of 19 November 2023, the Israel-Gaza war has taken a severe toll on journalists since Hamas launched its attack against Israel on 7 October 2023 and Israel declared war on the militant Palestinian group, launching strikes on the blockaded Gaza Strip. Journalists in Gaza face particularly  high risks as they try to cover the conflict during the Israeli ground assault, including devastating Israeli airstrikes, disrupted communications, supply shortages and extensive power outages.

subindicator: ILS2.1 - Telecommunications infrastructures damage or limitations
justification: As of November 11, public services are partially restored in Mexico post-Hurricane Otis. Approximately 93% of electricity services are back, while telecommunication services, ranging from 45% to 90%, have been restored, showing progress despite the initial disruptions.

The Inter American Press Association (IAPA) reported the eighth journalist killed in Haiti this year amid escalating gang violence and deliberate assaults on the media. Fritz Dorilas, from Radio Tele Megastar, was fatally shot near his Tabarre residence, northeast of Port-au-Prince, on November 5, as revealed by the association on Wednesday.

In September, two journalists lost their lives while covering violence in the impoverished Cite-Soleil neighborhood in Port-au-Prince. Roberson Alphonse, a prominent reporter for Le Nouvelliste newspaper, recently survived an assassination attempt, highlighting the perilous conditions journalists face while reporting in Haiti's volatile areas.

Dumesky Kersaint fearlessly delved into investigating violence in his gang-dominated Port-au-Prince neighborhood. Early on April 16, the 31-year-old radio reporter headed out to cover a recent shooting near his Carrefour-Feuilles home but didn't return. Hours later, his body, with a fatal gunshot wound to the forehead, was discovered on the street, alongside another victim of the incident he aimed to report on.

Following Moise’s assassination, political instability led to gang control over significant parts of the capital, creating an environment of lawlessness. Journalists operate under immense fear, fostering self-censorship despite efforts to report amid challenging conditions in an increasingly precarious and unregulated press climate.

In Ciudad Juarez, a newspaper photographer was discovered shot dead in a car's driver's seat, marking the fifth journalist killed in Mexico in 2023. Prosecutors confirmed the violent death in the notoriously dangerous border city, adding to the grim toll of journalist fatalities in the country this year.

Mexico has evolved into one of the most perilous regions globally for journalists, with three fatalities this year. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) reports at least 52 journalist killings in Mexico over five years. Last year marked a grim record, witnessing 15 deaths—the deadliest in recent memory for Mexican journalists, highlighting the escalating danger faced by media professionals.

Mexican photojournalist Ismael Villagomez, employed at El Heraldo de Juarez, was fatally shot while working as a ride-share driver in Ciudad Juarez. The incident occurred at approximately 1:30 a.m. in the notoriously violent border city, as confirmed by local authorities and his employer.

In Ciudad Juarez, a photographer working for a local newspaper was discovered fatally shot, as revealed by prosecutors on Thursday. The city, known for drug cartel dominance, witnessed the tragic death, further highlighting the persistent dangers within the region for journalists.

On 17 October 2023, unknown militants killed a journalist who is a member of the Journalists Syndicate near the Lebanon Falafel restaurant in the Alumma Park in Baghdad - Rusafa. The victim was born in 1967 and was a resident of Mosul.
On 14 July 2023, unknown militants opened fire at a journalist driving his car towards Diwaniya city. The journalist stated security forces did not intervene to protect him. There were no casualties.

adm1_eng_name: Peloponnese, Western Greece and the Ionian Islands
justification: On 14 June 2023, a boat carrying up to 750 migrants and refugees capsized inside the Greek Search and Rescue Zone. The Hellenic Coast Guard denied responsibility for the disaster and claimed that its offers of assistance were ignored. A joint investigation by Forensis, the Guardian, the Greek Council for Refugees, Alarm Phone, Solomon, and STRG_F (ARD/FUNK) found that the Coast Guard had attempted to “distort and manipulate evidence related to the incident.” This included confiscating survivors’ phones.

On 14 June 2023, a boat carrying up to 750 migrants and refugees capsized inside the Greek Search and Rescue Zone. On 16 and 17 June 2023, many survivors were transferred to Malakasa Reception and Identification Centre (RIC). The RIC is designed to temporarily hold irregular arrivals. Individuals are subject to strict movement restrictions. With their phones lost or confiscated, many struggled to contact friends and relatives to update them on the situation.

During the clashes on October 28, both Awami League and BNP supporters engaged in violence, injuring hundreds including dozens of journalists. Both parties have denied their involvement. While the authorities blame the BNP for the violence, the BNP has accused the government of infiltrating the gathering to initiate violence and discredit what they said was a peaceful movement.

On 28 October, opposition protesters allegedly attacked the residences of the Chief Justice and other judges, and approximately 30 journalists were assaulted by protesters and masked individuals riding on motorcycles, who are thought to have been ruling party supporters.

“The authorities in Minsk unleashed a new wave of persecution against the members of the democratic forces in Belarus. The attacks are aimed at intimidating and eliminating potential political opponents, especially ahead of the parliamentary elections in February next year,” EU High Representative Josep Borrell said in a statement.

On 13 November 2023, eight family members of photojournalist Yasser Qudih were killed when their house in southern Gaza was struck by four missiles. The incident occurred five days after a  report by HonestReporting—a group that monitors what it describes “ideological prejudice” in media coverage of Israel—raised questions about Qudih and three other photographers having prior knowledge of Hamas’ October 7 attack on Israel. Major media outlets rejected the claims. HonestReporting subsequently withdrew the accusations. Qudih survived the attack.

On 25 October 2023, Wael Al Dahdouh, Al-Jazeera’s bureau chief for Gaza, lost his wife, son, daughter, and grandson when an Israel airstrike hit the Nuseirat refugee camp in the center of Gaza, according to a statement from Al-Jazeera and Politico.

On 26 November 2023, several journalists reported being assaulted by Israeli forces while waiting in front of Ofer prison, located between Ramallah and Beituniya, to cover Israel’s release of Palestinian prisoners as part of the Hamas-Israel truce and prisoner exchange agreement, according to the Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate (PJS), the London-based news website The New Arab, and Al Araby TV.

On 26 November 2023, Journalists from Sky News Arabia, Firas Lutfi, and Raed El-Helw, informed the Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate that Israeli forces targeted them with tear gas and unidentified bullets while reporting from what they thought was a safe area, away from clashes in front of Ofer prison. They were wearing their media vests and informed the Israeli soldiers that they were members of the media. El-Helw was injured in his hand. El-Helw stated that it was a deliberate attack.

In the period between 1 December 2023 and 3 December 2023, since the end of the one-week temporary humanitarian truce, Israel has resumed its disproportionate air, artillery, and ground attacks in Gaza, motivated by mass murder plans. The deadly attacks have targeted different parts of the Gaza Strip.

 

Three Palestinian journalists have been killed in separate Israeli attacks, bringing the total number of journalists murdered in Israel’s ongoing war on Gaza to 73.

On December 1 the District Court of Kazanextended the detention period of Alsa Kurmasheva, a journalist of Tatar-Bashkir service of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty for two months. Alsu Kurmasheva is a citizen of USA and Russia, lives in Prague. She came to Russia on May 20. On June 2 she was detained at Kazan airport while waiting for flight to return to Czechia. Kurmasheva was fined for failing to comply with requirement to register American citizenship with Russian authorities.

This way the Russian side wants to show that the Russian Federation is supposedly "forever" on the occupied territories and that there is less resistance from the locals.

Pro-Kremlin resources spread information that the Kharkov authorities intend to start the construction of an underground school exclusively in their own interests - "for the sake of a good image and PR." He said that initiatives of this kind are made only in order to once again embezzle the budget, and schoolchildren in ordinary schools are allegedly not in danger. However, this is a fake.

Russian propaganda created fake news: a screenshot of news,allegedly published on the official website of the Polish government. The "news" reports that starting January 1, 2024, monetary assistance for Ukrainian refugees will be canceled. Russian propaganda is now spreading such fakes in order to create an additional factor of tension between Ukrainians and Poles against the background of the Polish-Ukrainian crisis related to the blocking of the border with Ukraine by Polish transporters and farmers.

Roshchina, who planned to travel to the occupied territories of eastern Ukraine via Russia to report on the situation there, left Ukraine for Poland on July 25 and was expected to reach the occupied territories three days later. 

She has been missing since August 3, and her current location is unknown.

The Committee to Protect Journalists on Monday condemned the 8.5-year sentence issued to Russian blogger Aleksandr Nozdrinov and called on Russian authorities to release him immediately and drop all charges against him.
The Committee to Protect Journalists condemns a Belarusian court’s Friday sentencing of journalist Alyaksandr Mantsevich to four years in prison for allegedly discrediting Belarus.
The Committee to Protect Journalists condemns the 72-hour detention of Belarusian journalist Andrei Tolchyn on extremism charges.
The Committee to Protect Journalists on Friday issued an urgent call for authorities to investigate allegations that journalists working in Latvia were targeted by state-sponsored hackers.

Russian Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu continues to falsely characterize Russian offensive efforts in Ukraine as part of an “active defense” in an effort to temper expectations about the Russian military’s ability to achieve operationally significant objectives.

Lithuania's intelligence agency (VSD) director Darius Jauniskis pointed out that Russian propaganda in Lithuania is gaining momentum.
The VSD's chief commented that a recent string of false bomb threats the country experienced in October was designed to cause confusion and uncertainty.

Ukraine’s IT Army emerged after Moscow’s February 2022 invasion. Comprising both international and local digital talents, this volunteer IT army collaborates with Ukraine’s defense ministry to target Russian digital infrastructure and websites. The volunteer IT army’s Telegram channel has counted upwards of 300,000 members.

UNHCR country brief for October 2023 points out that the regularization process continues in Ecuador, with people
continuing to apply for their visa despite several technical
issues in the online procedures. UNHCR, partners and other
UN agencies and programmes continue to support the
process

As part of the scientific literature exchange programs, the Russian Academy of Sciences plans to distribute propaganda literature in the world's libraries with the aim of further coverage in Kremlin resources.
This literature will "justify" the historical affiliation of the temporarily captured regions of Ukraine to the Russian Federation. The purpose of the provocation is to simulate support for Moscow's military aggression among scientists.

indicator: ILI3 - Vulnerability of specific groups within the context / safety and dignity of people accessing information
justification: According to the organisation, hate speech was present in political campaigns irrespective of the parties’ stance on the political spectrum. They discovered that anti-refugee hate speech was the most prominent narrative.

indicator: ILI3 - Vulnerability of specific groups within the context / safety and dignity of people accessing information
justification: High levels of hate speech during the latest election campaign were alarming, targeting multiple minority groups, including the LGBTQ community, refugees, liberals, and Roma.
