justification: On the morning of December 12, the largest mobile operator of Ukraine, which has 24 million subscribers, experienced a large-scale failure. The cause of a massive technical failure in the work of the largest mobile operator "Kyivstar" was a hacker attack on the network core. The Security Service of Ukraine has opened criminal proceedings on the fact of a cyber attack on one of the national mobile operators "Kyivstar".

The formal blockade of Russian television and radio channels in the Baltic states significantly limited the spread of propaganda, although it did not stop it completely. The common message that emerged after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine concerns refugees. Ukrainian refugees are allegedly ill-treated in Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia. The aim of this type of activities is social polarization, which is intended to lead to destabilization in countries.

Within the hybrid war against the West, the Kremlin uses the factor of Ukrainian displaced persons to destabilize the political and social situation in EU countries. With this aim, Russia is parasitizing anti-immigrant sentiments among right-wing and conservative circles of European societies.Russian propaganda discredits the image of Ukrainians in Europe.

subindicator: ILS4.4 - Deliberate communication shutdowns / restrictions from malicious actors
justification: The Committee to Protect Journalists has called for the immediate rescindment of the suspension of Namibia's New Era newspaper's managing editor, Johnathan Beukes, and the state-owned media outlet to operate independently. Beukes was suspended until October 31 due to an editorial critical of the judiciary, citing fear of reprisals.

Namibian police briefly detained freelance investigative reporters John Grobler and Nrupesh Soni on February 12, 2022, for allegedly trespassing at GoHunt Namibia Safaris' farm in the Omaheke region. The journalists used a drone to film elephants on private property, as reported by local media and CPJ.

Namibia's Minister of Information and Communication Technology, Peya Mushelenga, has emphasized the need for improved cybersecurity defense mechanisms, digital resilience, online safety best practices, and the transformative potential of digitalization at the 7th National Information and Communication Technology Summit in Windhoek. She highlighted the importance of protection for application, network, and data security.

Namibia's New Era newspaper's Managing Editor, Johnathan Beukes, was suspended from work on October 2nd after publishing an editorial criticizing the judiciary. The International Federation of Journalists (IFJ) and Namibia Media Professionals Union (NAMPU) condemn Beukes' removal as a deliberate attack on media freedom and urge authorities to reinstate him promptly.
In Burundi, on 15 September, the Government dismissed rumours of an attempted coup d’état following the deployment of special forces in front of the premises of Burundi National Radio and Television.

On 15 December 2023, Samer Abu Daqqa, a camera operator for Al-Jazeera Arabic, was killed by a drone strike while covering the aftermath of Israeli strikes on a UN school sheltering displaced people in the center of Khan Yunis, southern Gaza. He was trapped with other injured people in the school, which was surrounded by Israeli forces, and was unable to be evacuated for treatment. His colleague, Al-Jazeera bureau chief Wael Al Dahdouh, was also injured in the same strike.

Ola Atallah, a Palestinian female freelance journalist who contributed to multiple media outlets, was killed in an Israeli airstrike on the house in which she and her family was taking refuge, in the El-Daraj area of Gaza city in northern Gaza on 9 December 2023, according to Arabi 21, Anadolu news agency, and the Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate. Those sources said that Atallah was killed with nine members of her family, including her brother and her uncles.

On 3 December 2023, Hassan Farajallah, who held a senior position for the Hamas-affiliated Al-Quds TV, was killed in an Israeli bombardment in the Gaza Strip, according to the Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate and the International Federation of Journalists.

On 3 December 2023, Shaima El-Gazzar, a Palestinian journalist for Al-Majedat network, was killed along with her family members in an Israeli airstrike on Rafah city in the southern Gaza Strip, according to the Beirut-based press freedom group SKeyes and the Cairo-based media outlet Darb.

On 1 December 2023, Abdullah Darwish, a Palestinian cameraman for the Hamas-affiliated Al-Aqsa TV, was killed in an Israeli airstrike in the Gaza Strip, according to the Amman-based news outlet Roya News, the Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate, and the International Federation of Journalists.

On December 1, 2023, Montaser Al-Sawaf, a Palestinian cameraman for Anadolu Agency, was killed in Israeli airstrikes in the Gaza Strip, as confirmed by Anadolu Agency, Middle East Monitor, and the International Federation of Journalists.

On 1 December 2023, Adham Hassouna, a Palestinian freelance journalist and media professor at Gaza and Al-Aqsa universities, was killed, along with several members of his family in an Israeli airstrike in the city of Gaza, as reported by the Ramallah-based Palestinian news network SHFA and the Beirut-based press freedom group SKeyes, and the Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate.

On 24 November 2023, Mostafa Bakeer, a Palestinian journalist and cameraperson for the Hamas-affiliated Al-Aqsa TV, was killed in an Israeli airstrike in Rafah, southern Gaza, according to the Hamas-affiliated Al-Aqsa radio, the Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate, and the International Federation of Journalists.

On 23 November 2023, Mohamed Mouin Ayyash, a Palestinian journalist and a freelance photographer, was killed in an Israeli airstrike on his home in Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza, along with 20 members of his family, according to the Amman-based news outlet Roya News, the Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate, and the Palestinian Authority’s official news agency Wafa.

On 22 November 2023, Mohamed Nabil Al-Zaq, a Palestinian journalist and a social media manager for the Hamas-affiliated Al-Quds TV, was killed in an Israeli airstrike on Shejaiya in northern Gaza, according to the Amman-based news outlet Roya News, the Ramallah-based news website Wattan TV, the Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate, and the International Federation of Journalists.

On 21 November 2023, Farah Omar, a Lebanese reporter for the Hezbollah-affiliated Al-Mayadeen TV channel, was killed by an Israeli strike in the Tayr Harfa area in southern Lebanon, close to the border with Israel. She was reporting on escalating hostilities across the Lebanese-Israeli border and gave a live update an hour before her death. Rabih Al Maamari, a Lebanese cameraperson for the Hezbollah-affiliated Al-Mayadeen TV channel, was killed by an Israeli strike along with his colleague Farah Omar.

On 20 November 2023, Ayat Khadoura, a Palestinian freelance journalist and podcast presenter, was killed along with an unknown number of family members in an Israeli airstrike on her home in Beit Lahya in northern Gaza. Khadoura shared videos on social media about the situation in Gaza, including a November 6, 2023 video, where she said, “We had big dreams but our dream now is to be killed in one piece so they know who we are.

On 18 November 2023, Abdelhalim Awad, a Palestinian media worker and driver for the Hamas-affiliated Al-Aqsa TV, was killed in a strike on his home in the Gaza Strip, according to the London-based Al-Ghad TV, the Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate, and the Beirut-based press freedom group SKeyes. Awad had been working full-time since the beginning of the war in Khan Yunis and had left to visit his family last week, his colleague Ziad AlMokayyed told CPJ via messaging app.

Mossab Ashour, a Palestinian photographer, was killed during an attack on the Nuseirat refugee camp in the Gaza Strip but his death was not reported until 18 November 2023, soon after his body was discovered, according to the Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate, TRT Arabi, and Anadolu Agency.

On November 13, 2023, Ahmed Fatima, a photographer for the Egypt-based Al Qahera News TV and a media worker with Press House-Palestine, Fatima was killed in a strike in Gaza, according to Al Qahera News TV, the Egypt-based Ahram Online, the Palestinians Journalists’ Syndicate, and the Amman-based news outlet Roya News.

On November 13, 2023, Yaacoub Al-Barsh, executive director of the local Namaa Radio, was killed after sustaining injuries on November 12, 2023, from an Israeli airstrike on his home in northern Gaza, according to the Beirut-based press freedom group SKeyes, the Ramallah-based Palestinian news network SHFA, and the Palestinian press freedom group MADA.

On November 10, 2023, Ahmed Al-Qara, a photojournalist who worked for Al-Aqsa University and was also a freelancer, was killed in a strike at the entrance of Khuza’a town, east of the southern city of Khan Yunis, according to the Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate and the Cairo-based Al-Dostor newspaper.

On November 7, 2023, Yahya Abu Manih, a journalist with Hamas-affiliated Al-Aqsa radio channel, Abu Manih was killed in a strike in the Gaza strip, according to the Amman-based news outlet Roya News, Al-Jazeera, and the Beirut-based press freedom group SKeyes.

On November 7, 2023, Mohamed Abu Hassira, a journalist for the Palestinian Authority-run Wafa news agency, was killed in a strike on his home in Gaza along with 42 family members, according to the Palestinian Authority’s official news agency Wafa, the London-based news website The New Arab, and the Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate.

Mohamed Al Jaja was a media worker and the organizational development consultant at Press House-Palestine, which owns Sawa news agency in Gaza and promotes press freedom and independent media. On November 5, 2023, he was killed in a strike on his home along with his wife and two daughters in the Al-Naser neighborhood in northern Gaza, according to the London-based news website The New Arab, the Beirut-based press freedom group SKeyes, and the Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate.

On November 2, 2023, Mohamad Al-Bayyari, a Palestinian journalist with the Hamas affiliated Al-Aqsa TV channel, was killed in an Israeli airstrike on Gaza City, according to the Amman-based news outlet Roya News, the Palestinian Authority’s official news agency Wafa, the Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate, and the International Federation of Journalists.

On October 25, 2023, Jamal Al-Faqaawi, a Palestinian journalist for the Islamic Jihad-affiliated Mithaq Media Foundation, was killed in an Israeli airstrike on his home in Khan Yunis in southern Gaza, according to Al-Jazeera,  the Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate, the Palestinian News Network, and the International Federation of Journalists.

Every month, specialists of the cyber department of the SBU record more than a thousand destructive information attacks on Ukrainian society. The spread of disinformation to the general public in the modern world has become not only commonplace, but also a threat to reality, which can cause significant damage to the national security of Ukraine.

Mustafa Alkharouf, a photographer with the Turkish state-owned Anadolu Agency, was covering Friday prayers near Al-Aqsa Mosque in East Jerusalem on December 15, 2023 when a group of Israeli police and soldiers attacked him. Soldiers initially brandished their weapons at Alkharouf, punched him, and then threw him to the ground, kicking him. Alkharouf sustained severe blows, resulting in injuries to his face and body, and was transported by ambulance and treated at Makassed Hospital in East Jerusalem.

On November 13, 2023, Issam Mawassi, Al-Jazeera videographer was injured after two Israeli missiles struck near journalists in Yaroun in southern Lebanon covering clashes, which also resulted in damage to the journalists’ cars in the area, according to multiple media reports, some of which show the journalists live on air the minute the second missile hit the area. Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) reached out to Mawassi via a messaging app but didn’t receive any response.

On November 2, 2023, Mohammed Abu Hatab, a journalist and correspondent for the Palestinian Authority-funded broadcaster Palestine TV, was killed along with 11 members of his family in an Israeli airstrike on their home in Khan Yunis, southern Gaza Strip, according to the Palestinian Authority’s official news agency Wafa and the Amman-based news outlet Roya News.

Around 5 November 2023 (as reported), the two offices of Darfur 24 electronic newspaper in Nyala and Khartoum have been looted and damaged by unknown perpetrators. Darfur 24’s investigation into the case of its two looted offices revealed that the attackers looted 6 laptop computers, photographic equipment, sabotaged satellite communications network equipment, embedded software components and two photocopying printers.

The introduction of Safety of Rwanda (Asylum and Immigration) Bill” to parliament in UK comes in response to the Supreme Court’s 15/11 ruling on the UK’s deal with Rwanda, which found Rwanda is not a safe third country to send asylum seekers. More than a dozen opposition members, two journalists and two commentators currently sit in jail for expressing opinions and criticism of the Rwandan government.

Areas encompassing about 30 per cent of the Gaza Strip (excluding the orders to evacuate the areas north of Wadi Gaza) have been marked for evacuation on the Israeli military’s online map. Islam Bader, a Palestinian reporter and presenter for the Hamas-affiliated Al-Aqsa channel, and a contributor to multiple media outlets including the Qatari-funded Al-Araby TV, was injured in the right shoulder and hip in an Israeli airstrike on Block 2 of the Jabalia refugee camp, northern Gaza, on December 19, 2023. His colleague Mohamed Ahmed, a Palestinian reporter for the Hamas-affiliated Shehab agency and photographer for the Hamas-affiliated Al-Aqsa channel, was injured in the left thigh in the same strike.

Mohamed Balousha, a reporter for the Emirati-owned Dubai-based Al Mashahd TV, was shot in the thigh while reporting on the war from northern Gaza on December 16, 2023. The bullet was fired by an Israeli sniper. Balousha said in a video about his injury that he lost consciousness for about 30 minutes after “six hours of agony”. Al Mashhad said that Israeli forces intercepted the ambulances sent to evacuate him, delaying his transfer to a hospital for treatment.

Assem Kamal Moussa, a Palestinian journalist who produced visual and written news reports for the local privately owned news website Palestine Now, was killed in an Israeli airstrike on Khan Yunis, southern Gaza on December 17, 2023, according to his outlet, Lebanon’s Hezbollah-affiliated broadcaster Al-Mayadeen, and the Hamas-affiliated Al-Aqsa radio channel.

On December 17, 2023, Haneen Kashtan, a Palestinian journalist who contributed to multiple media outlets including the local Fatah-affiliated TV Al-Kofiya, the local privately owned Baladna Web TV (launched by journalists in 2017), and others, was killed in an Israeli airstrike on Nuseirat refugee camp in northern Gaza, along with other family members, according to the Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate, Al-Jazeera, and the Cairo-based Youm7.

On December 19, 2023, Adel Zorob, a Palestinian freelance journalist who worked with multiple media outlets, including the Hamas affiliated Al-Aqsa Voice Radio, was killed in an Israeli airstrike on his home in Rafah, southern Gaza, along with 25 family members.

Zorob posted Gaza war news on his Facebook page and on WhatsApp news groups. The Zorob family were among the few Palestinians in Gaza who remained in their own homes in a war that has displaced some 1.9 million people.

Abdallah Alwan, a Palestinian media worker and voice-over specialist who contributed to multiple media outlets including the Al-Jazeera owned platform Midan, Mugtama magazine and Al-Jazeera, and was a radio host for the Islamic University’s Holy Quran Radio, was killed in an Israeli airstrike on his home in Jabalia on December 18, 2023, according to his outlet Midan, the Hamas-affiliated Al-Aqsa Radio, the local Palestinian newspaper Al-Hadath, and Jordan’s Amman-based Roya TV.

Rwandan authorities and their proxies are using violence, judicial mechanisms, and intimidation to try to silence criticism from Rwandans living around the world. Rwandans living abroad practice self-censorship, refrain from political activism, and live in fear of traveling, being attacked, or seeing their relatives in Rwanda targeted.

Journalists and those who disagree with the government's narrative faced threats, arrests, and expulsion. Solomon Shumye, a talk show host from Addis Ababa, was arrested in May. He was among 19 journalists, including Gobeze Sisay and Meaza Mohammed, detained during a government crackdown in the Amhara region. Gobeze and Meaza were released, but later rearrested in September.

subindicator: ILS4.4 - Deliberate communication shutdowns / restrictions from malicious actors
justification: The Cyber and Data Protection Act of 2021 has exacerbated Zimbabwean rights, with internet slowed down during rallies and demonstrations by opposition parties in February and March 2022.

On January 7, 2024, Hamza Al Dahdouh, a Palestinian journalist and camera operator for Al-Jazeera, and the son of Al-Jazeera Gaza bureau chief Wael Al Dahdouh, was killed in an Israeli drone strike along with freelance journalist Mustafa Thuraya, according to Al-Jazeera Arabic. They were driving to an assignment in southern Gaza when the strike occurred, according to Al-Jazeera and the BBC.

On December 29, 2023, Jabr Abu Hadrous, a Palestinian journalist and a reporter for the Hamas-affiliated Quds Al-Youm broadcaster, was killed in an Israeli airstrike on his home in Nuseirat refugee camp, northern Gaza, along with seven members of his family, according to Al-Jazeera, Hezbollah-affiliated Al-Mayadeen, and the privately owned government-affiliated Al-Ghad newspaper in Jordan.

On 24 December 2023, Mohamad Al-Iff, a Palestinian journalist and photographer for the Hamas government-owned local newspaper and news agency Al-Rai, was killed in Israeli airstrikes on Gaza City, northern Gaza, along with an unspecified number of family members, according to the Beirut-based press freedom group SKeyes, the Qatar-funded London-based pan Arab newspaper Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, and the Hamas-affiliated Quds Network. Al-Iff’s cousin, journalist Mohamed Azzaytouniyah, was killed in the same strikes, according to a tweet by Al-Iff’s cousin Hammam.

On December 24, 2023, Ahmad Jamal Al Madhoun, a Palestinian journalist and deputy director of the Hamas government-owned local newspaper and news agency Al-Rai and the director of visual content at the agency, was killed in an Israeli airstrike on northern Gaza, according to the Hamas-affiliated Quds Network, the Qatar-funded London-based pan Arab newspaper Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, and Anadolu news agency.

On December 23, 2023, Mohamed Naser Abu Huwaidi, a 29-year-old Palestinian journalist working for the privately owned Al-Istiklal newspaper, was killed in an Israeli airstrike on the Shajaiah area in northern Gaza while covering the aftermath of the airstrikes, according to the Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate, the Qatar-funded London-based pan Arab newspaper Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, the Beirut-based press freedom group SKeyes, and the Cairo-based independent website Daaarb.

On December 22, 2023, Mohamed Khalifeh, a media worker and director at the Hamas-affiliated Al-Aqsa TV channel was killed in an Israeli airstrike on his home in Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza, along his wife and three of his children, according to his outlet, Anadolu news agency, the Lebanese Hezbollah-affiliated Al-Mayadeen TV, and the privately owned news channel Al-Ghad TV.

On December 23, 2023, Khader Marquez, a cameraman for Lebanon’s Hezbollah-owned TV channel Al-Manar was injured after shrapnel from an Israeli missile hit his car on the Khardali road of south Lebanon, injuring his left eye, according to Al-Manar correspondent Ali Shoeib, who was with Marquez, posted about the incident on social media, and spoke to the privately-owned Beirut-based Al-Jadeed TV.

On September 30, security force members arrested Samira Sabou, a blogger and journalist, at her mother’s home in Niamey. According to Amnesty International, “Men in civilian clothes, presenting themselves as security officers, came to arrest Samira,” her husband said.

In May, police fired rubber bullets at journalists covering a protest in Windhoek, while in February, two freelance investigative reporters were briefly detained for trespassing at a private farm while investigating the illegal sale of pregnant wild elephants to unidentified groups in Dubai.

In February 2022, Namibia's first lady won 250,000 Namibian dollars in a defamation suit against opposition party figure Abed Hishoono, who was accused of spreading false content about her. She later apologized and declined compensation after Hishoono apologized after showing remorse.

UNHCR Migration situation monitoring in Honduras as November 2023  showed a trend: migrants entering Hondurean territory  are unaware of the amnesty payment of the fine for irregular entry and
they may seek to evade controls immigration and police.

justification: Zimbabwe faces severe internet access limitations due to economic crises and inadequate infrastructure. The Syrian Network for Human Rights (SNHR) today released its 13th annual report. The report provides details of the most notable violations against medical personnel and media workers, noting that four medical personnel, including one woman, were killed in 2023, all at the hands of Syrian regime forces, while three media workers were killed this year: one by Syrian regime forces, and two by other parties.

On January 14, 2024, Yazan al-Zuweidi, a Palestinian journalist and camera operator for the privately owned Cairo-based broadcaster Al-Ghad, was killed, along with his brother and cousin, in an Israeli airstrike on Beit Hanoun in northern Gaza while al-Zuweidi was on his way to see what happened to his home in the aftermath of heavy bombing. Al-Zuweidi, 27, had been working with Al-Ghad for six years, and covered the war and various other events in Gaza.

Namibia's Communications Regulatory Authority (CRAN) has imposed mandatory SIM card registration from January 1, 2023, to comply with Section 77 of the Communications Act. Existing customers have a 12-month window until December 31, 2023, while new SIM cards must be registered within three months of purchase. This move is part of a global initiative to enhance security and digital identity.

Dimension Data Namibia, a subsidiary of Ohlthaver & List, launched its first in-country hosted security platform on 21 September 2023. The platform combines physical firewalls, network security, threat detection, prevention, and incident response with a software-defined wide area network (SD-WAN), allowing end-users to pre-emptively respond to and prevent cyberattacks.

Namibia's Minister of Information and Communication Technology, Peya Mushelenga, has emphasized the need for improved cybersecurity defense mechanisms, digital resilience, online safety best practices, and the transformative potential of digitalization at the 7th National Information and Communication Technology Summit in Windhoek. She highlighted the importance of protection for application, network, and data security.

Namibia, a rapidly developing country with a growing digital economy, is facing a surge in cybersecurity issues such as phishing, malware, and data breaches. As businesses and individuals increasingly rely on technology, it is crucial to be aware of these risks and take steps to mitigate them. In 2022, Namibia experienced a 40% increase in reported cyberattacks, according to Kamal Tour, acting head of cybercrime programmes in Africa for the UNODC.

The Zambian government has directed the Information, Communication and Technology Authority (ZICTA) to enhance cyber security services, according to Technology and Science Minister Felix Mutati. He emphasized the need for advanced technical knowhow to keep systems ahead of hackers and appreciate the ongoing development of innovative digital solutions.

President Hakainde Hichilema plans to review the controversial Cyber Security and Cyber Crime law, enacted by the previous administration. The law aims to combat cybercrime, coordinate cybersecurity matters, develop skills, promote social media use, and protect national critical infrastructure. However, it faced opposition from civil society organizations and opposition parties.

Liquid C2, a subsidiary of Cassava Technologies, has established the Zambian Cyber Security Fusion Centre in Lusaka, marking the third such facility in Africa. The Zambian government reported over 10 million cyber attacks in 2021, including mobile money scams, social media account hijacking, and fake product promotions. The Minister of Technology and Science, Felix Mutati, emphasized the growing threat of cybercrime.

The latest cyber security report, 'The Evolving Cyber Security Landscape in Africa 2022', reveals a significant increase in cyberattacks against large enterprises across Kenya, South Africa, and Zambia. Kenyan businesses experienced an 82% increase in such attacks, while South African businesses saw a 62% increase and Zambian businesses saw a 62% increase.

The Electronic Transactions and Cyber Security Act, enacted in Malawi in 2016, aims to regulate electronic transactions, protect against cybercrime, and ensure digital communications security. However, concerns exist about its potential to suppress dissent in Southern African countries.

Malawian journalist Gregory Gondwe was arrested on April 5, 2022, on a charge of spamming under Section 91 of the Electronic Transaction and Cyber Security Act of 2016. Gondwe was arrested after publishing an article on alleged state capture by British businessperson Zuneth Sattar. The act states that transmitting unsolicited electronic information for illegal trade or commerce is an offense, and a conviction can result in a fine of K2,000,000 and imprisonment for five years.

The Digital Malawi Project, led by TakenoLab, aims to enhance computer skills in schools in the district, with plans to expand to more schools. Supported by an NGO and the Dowa district council, the project aims to boost digital literacy and proficiency among youth, enhancing problem-solving and critical thinking skills. It will create tech-savvy youth, boost employability, and contribute to the country's digital economy.

The Public Private Partnership Commission (PPPC) in Malawi has successfully trained 10930 youths and women in digital skills, surpassing the target of 5,000 beneficiaries. The Digital Skills Development and Innovation Initiative, funded by the World Bank through nine tech hubs, aims to address Malawi's digital literacy and advanced ICT skills gaps, strengthen the digital innovation and entrepreneurship ecosystem, and promote job creation, entrepreneurship, and creativity, especially for the youth.

On July 26, 2023, the Ntha Foundation held a Mass Digital Literacy Awareness Campaign in Mangochi, Malawi, under The Digital Malawi Project. The initiative, funded by The World Bank, was implemented by The Public Private Partnership commission and The Public Private Partnership commission. The campaign aimed to bridge the digital divide and equip individuals with the necessary skills to thrive in the digital world.

Malawi's Minister of Information and Digitalization, Gospel Kazako, announced plans to train 300 traditional leaders with basic digital skills and devices through the Malawi Communications Regulatory Authority (Macra). The government aims to ensure access and affordable internet services in the country. The digitally enlightened leaders will serve as digital ambassadors, helping pass knowledge and make the community digitally literate.

Malawi's Minister of Information, Moses Kunkuyu, acknowledged low ICT skills uptake among the country's population. A 2021 study by the Public Private Partnership Commission revealed that 54% of men lack foundational digital skills, and 74% of women lack basic digital literacy. Kunkuyu emphasized the need for further action to improve the situation during the launch of Malawi Seeds for the Future.

ICT, Postal and Courier Services minister Tatenda Mavetera has urged organizations to enhance their clients' digital literacy to accommodate new disruptive technologies, particularly artificial intelligence (AI). She stressed the need for government and private sector input to ensure value from AI implementation. Mavetera highlighted the legal aspects of consumer protection and the readiness of Zimbabwe for AI, which she will consult with at the Computer Society of Zimbabwe annual congress.

The ICT ministry in Bulawayo has launched a digital giant project to ensure all Zimbabweans have access to digital services, regardless of their location. The project includes an ICT laboratory at every school in Waterford and Emakhandeni suburbs, a public finance management system centre, a digital training center for civil servants, and a data recovery site at the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe offices.

The Information Communication Technology Postal and Courier Services ministry has commissioned two advanced ICT labs at Domboramwari High and Epworth Primary School in Harare to enhance learning methods and student collaboration, fulfilling President Emmerson Mnangagwa's mandate to ensure no one is left behind in the digital age.

CHENHAKA Trust executive director Taurayi Moyo has urged artists to improve their literacy skills to meet local and global standards. The trust, in partnership with the National Arts Council of Zimbabwe, conducted a 15-day arts management and business value addition boot camp for 30 industry players at Chancellor Primary School Arts Centre in Mutare. Moyo emphasized the need for artists to enhance digital literacy and skills to bridge the digital divide through virtual events.

Zimbabwe's Minister Mavetera has expressed concern over the digital divide between rural and urban areas, stating that the government is working on strategies to make internet services more affordable. The aim is to provide access to these services to the majority of Zimbabweans by 2030, as the country aims to become an upper-middle-income society.

The World Bank Group's report, 'Digital Economy Diagnostic Eswatini', highlights the urgent need for the government to establish comprehensive policies and implementation plans for digital skills development in Eswatini. The report is part of the Digital Economy for Africa Initiative, which aims to have every African individual, business, and government digitally enabled by 2030, as part of the African Union's Digital Moonshot for Africa.

The Ericsson Mobility Report predicts a 3% annual growth in mobile subscriptions in Sub-Saharan Africa, from 940 million in 2023 to 1.1 billion in 2029. The report highlights 5G as the fastest-growing subscription type, with Madagascar being one of the first African countries to commercially launch 5G.

Madagascar's microfinance institution, Première Agence de Microfinance (PAMF), has launched a service in 2021 that enables three million Facebook users to apply for credit or open a savings account, leveraging the social network's popularity among Malagasy.

Professor Anicia Peters, Chief Executive Officer of the National Commission of Research Science and Technology, highlighted the issue of digital literacy in Namibia despite the growing opportunities in Artificial Intelligence. She spoke at Youth Quake Namibia's annual event, which aimed to promote digital rights among the youth and empower them in the digital era.

International Literacy Day, celebrated annually on 8 September, emphasizes the significance of literacy as a fundamental human right and aims to foster a more literate, equal, and inclusive society. Digital literacy has become a crucial aspect of education, equipping learners with writing, reading, and technical skills.

Mozambican journalist João Chamusse was found lifeless outside his Maputo residence, believed to be murdered by unidentified assailants. Local media reports that Chamusse's desperate cries for help were heard during the early hours of Thursday. The investigative process revealed a gruesome scene with a head wound, a machete, and a gardening hoe in close proximity.

The killing of journalist Chamusse adds to the list of journalist assaults and enforced disappearances in Mozambique, with several cases remaining unresolved. Ibraimo Mbaruco was kidnapped in April 2020, and Paulo Machava, editor-in-chief and senior investigative reporter for Diario de Noticias news website, was killed in August 2015 by unknown assailants. No one has been held accountable for these incidents.

On Mozambican Journalists' Day, women in the media are voicing concerns about challenges and sexual harassment they face, highlighting that the profession is often undervalued, particularly for those starting their careers, according to journalist Cléusia Chirindza.

The Mozambican chapter of MISA has condemned police harassment of journalist Antonio Zacarias, who works for the weekly paper "Magazine Independente". The incident occurred in Maxixe, Inhambane, where Zacarias was covering a conflict between municipal police and informal vendors. The police were attempting to confiscate their goods, claiming their activities were illegal.

The Committee to Protect Journalists has called for an investigation into the assault of two broadcast reporters by police officers from Mozambique's National Criminal Investigation Service (SERNIC) in Maputo. The incident occurred on August 4 while covering the funeral of another police officer who had committed suicide. The journalists were unable to report freely and without fear, highlighting the need for greater transparency and accountability in the country's press freedom system.

Chissale's forced disappearance follows numerous documented cases of harassment, threats, and arbitrarily detained journalists covering conflict between government forces and the Islamist armed group al-Shabab.

Since February 2019, Mustapha Bendjama, the editor of Le Provincial newspaper, has faced persistent police detention and undergone interrogation on at least 35 occasions. In Annaba, eastern Algeria, authorities continually exert pressure on him, with allies citing his ongoing challenges to government policies. This situation raises concerns about the safety and well-being of journalists in the region.

Canadian-Algerian researcher Raouf Farrah and Algerian journalist Mustapha Bendjama have received two-year prison sentences from a court in Constantine, Algeria. The charges include publishing sensitive state information. Additionally, Farrah was found guilty on Tuesday of receiving funds from foreign powers to undermine state security. These convictions highlight the precarious environment for journalists and researchers in Algeria, raising concerns about their safety and freedom of expression.

On Wednesday evening, Egyptian authorities released 32 pre-trial detainees, among them three female journalists, after nearly two years of imprisonment. This development is significant in a country that holds the dubious distinction of being the world's third-worst jailer of journalists, emphasizing the challenges to press freedom and journalist safety.

Women Journalists Without Chains (WJWC) applauds the release of three female journalists detained in 2022 by Egyptian authorities. While recognizing this positive step, WJWC asserts that it falls short in adequately addressing persistent press freedom challenges in Egypt. The announcement of Manal Ajrama, Hala Fahmy, and Safaa Al-Korbigi's release was made by Khaled El-Balshy, head of the Egyptian Journalists Syndicate, on Wednesday, February 7, although the reasons for their release remain unclear.

On January 3, police conducted a raid and search at the residence of Sassi, a reporter for Qatari broadcaster Al-Jazeera in Tunis. Reports and Al-Jazeera's Tunisia bureau chief, Lotfi Hajji, confirmed the arrest, noting the confiscation of Sassi's laptop, phone, books, as well as the phones of his wife and children. This incident raises concerns about the safety and freedom of journalists in the region.

On 12 February 2024, Alaa Al-Hams, a 35-year-old Palestinian journalist for the local Palestinian News Agency SND succumbed to her injuries after being seriously wounded in an Israeli airstrike on her family house in Rafah city, southern Gaza Strip, which resulted in the tragic loss of ten members of her family on 2 December 2023, according to Palestine Chronicle, the Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate (PJS), and the Cairo-Based Ahram online.

On 12 February 2024, Angam Ahmad Edwan, a Palestinian journalist who worked for the Libyan TV channel February, was killed in an Israeli airstrike on her home in Jabalia city, northern Gaza Strip, according to her channel, the Cairo-Based Ahram online , the Turkish state-owned Anadolu Agency, and Palestine Chronicle.

subindicator: ILS2.2 - Accessible, safe and accurate information
justification: In Jordan, internet access varies based on socioeconomic status, gender, and geography. The taxation of mobile internet service is considered a key barrier to access, particularly for low-income individuals. Prices for internet service have dropped in recent years due to increased competition, despite the fact that the sales tax on internet service increased from 8 percent to 16 percent in 2017. The most inexpensive fiber-optic plan of 200 Mbps with a major service provider costs 20 Jordanian dinars per month.

Internet freedom in Jordan remains restricted. Access to the internet has improved significantly in recent years, although concerns about state surveillance of online activity persist. Online journalists, activists, and social media users can be prosecuted for their criticism of the government, based on several laws that penalize legitimate expression online. Journalists are pressured to remove online content, and authorities frequently issue gag orders to limit media coverage of politically sensitive topics.

subindicator: ILS4.4 - Deliberate communication shutdowns / restrictions from malicious actors
justification: In December 2022, authorities restricted internet access in several cities in the south of Jordan during protests. The internet shutdowns occurred in Ma’an and Karak amid demonstrations by truck drivers who were protesting the increase in fuel prices.

Internet shutdowns in Maan and Karak resulted in restricted Internet access on mobile phones and 4G services, whereas landline connections have not been disrupted.

According to the study, 17 per cent of Jordanians only read news headlines, while 32 per cent said that they mainly follow online comments on the news, and that their personal opinions are affected by them.

The first publicly confirmed case of Pegasus being used in Jordan occurred in March 2021, with the hacking of Jordanian human rights lawyer Hala Ahed, revealed in January 2022 by Access Now and Front Line Defenders.

Communication minister Moussa Bocar Thiam suspended Walf TV and Walfadjri’s radio station, Walf FM, of their licences for good on 4 February, shortly after the TV channel discovered that its signal had been cut.

On 8 February 2024, Nafez Abdel Jawad, a Palestinian director for the official Palestine Television station, Palestine TV, was killed along with his son in an Israeli missile strike on the house they were staying in Deir al-Balah in the Gaza Strip. Additionally, the missile killed 14 people, including 5 children. Responding to an inquiry from CNN on the killing of Abdel Jawad, the Israel Defense Forces stated that it “takes all operationally feasible measures to mitigate harm to civilians.”

On 29 January 2024, Mohammed Atallah, a 24-year-old Palestinian editor for the local Al-Resalah news website and a writer for the regional independent website Raseef22, was killed in an Israeli airstrike on Beach refugee camp in northern Gaza City, along with an unidentified number of family members, according to a tweet by Raseef22 that included his last voice message, the local news agency Safa, the Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate, and the International Federation of Journalists.

On 25 January 2024, Iyad El-Ruwagh, a Palestinian journalist who worked as a host for the Hamas-affiliated Al-Aqsa Voice Radio, was killed in an Israeli airstrike on Nuseirat camp in northern Gaza, along with four of his children, according to multiple media reports, a tweet by his outlet, the Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate, and the Beirut-based press freedom group SKeyes.

El-Ruwagh was buried on 26 January 2024, according to Al-Jazeera.

On 28 December 2023, Ahmed Khaireddine, a Palestinian journalist and a cameraman for the Hamas-affiliated Quds Al-Youm TV, and a reporter for the Hamas-affiliated Quds feed, was killed in an Israeli airstrike on his family home in Beit Lahiya, northern Gaza, along with 12 family members, including his uncle Mohamed Khaireddine, according to the Palestinian Authority-run broadcaster Palestine Today, the Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate, and Al-Jazeera.

subindicator: ILS4.4 - Deliberate communication shutdowns / restrictions from malicious actors
justification: Mobile Internet access was disconnected on 4 February for the second time in less than nine months. The statement issued by communication minister Moussa Bocar Thiam, referring to the “dissemination of many hateful and subversive messages relayed on social media,” was sadly similar to the one issued last June.

Earlier in the day, gendarmes harassed and aggressed three reporters covering the protests organised by opposition candidates in response to the presidential election’s postponement, announced the day before by President Macky Sall.

Gendarmes arrested Mame Ndack Mbacké, a reporter for the Agora TV press group, and Khadija Ndatté Diouf, a privately-owned TV channel ITV reporter, who had just interviewed politicians and government opponents. They were bundled into one vehicle and their reporting equipment was seized.

In Senegal, journalists are often the victims of arrests and dozen were arrested in the course of their work from July 2022 to August 2023 and attacks by either the security forces or politicians, political activists or their supporters.

Pape Alé Niang, the editor of the Dakarmatin news site, was placed in pre-trial detention on 29 July 2023, on a charge of “calling for insurrection” in the comments he made in a live broadcast on his website’s Facebook page about opposition politician Ousmane Sonko’s arrest on 28 July.

subindicator: ILS4.4 - Deliberate communication shutdowns / restrictions from malicious actors
justification: Access to the Internet and social media has also been drastically restricted since yesterday the 1st of June 2023, as many journalists have reported. Members of the KeepitOn coalition, which monitors Internet cuts worldwide, have reported problems connecting with WhatsApp, Twitter, Facebook and Instagram via the Orange and Tigo networks.

The director of Coton, Saleck Ag Jiddou, a community radio station in Ansongo, a small town in northern Mali’s Gao region, and Moustapha Koné, a Coton presenter, was abducted by members of an unidentified armed group while driving to Gao on 7 November with two other journalists. Naata community radio reporter Abdoul Aziz Djibrilla, was killed when the gunmen opened fire on their car while Harouna Attino, a journalist with Alafia, another Ansongo-based community radio station, was wounded.

Shot dead in an ambush by an armed gang in northern Mali, Abdoul Aziz Djibrilla worked for community radio, one of the most important sources of news in the Sahel, and embodied the battle waged by local reporters to inform the population in conflict zones. He was killed instantly when the vehicle in which he was travelling to Gao was fired on by an armed gang that had yet to be identified.

On 30 September, Samira Sabou, President of the Association of Bloggers for Active Citizenship (ABCA), was arrested at her home by members of the police force dressed in civilian dress because she posted a confidential defence ministry document without any comment on her Facebook page, on which she has more than 290,000 followers.

The editor of the newspaper Le Témoin de l’Histoire, Soufiane Mana Hassan, told RSF that on 28 July unidentified individuals threatened him on the street near his house, telling him to watch out for what he published in his paper and on his social media. A few days later, blogger and journalist Samira Sabou was questioned by a member of the military, who contacted her by phone, criticizing one of her social media posts.

On 19 August, independent journalists Amaury Hauchard and Stanislas Poyet, who are based in Niamey and contribute to several international media outlets, were attacked physically and verbally while covering a gathering of “volunteers for the homeland.” Poyet’s passport, as well as the journalists’ photo and radio equipment, were stolen.

subindicator: ILS4.4 - Deliberate communication shutdowns / restrictions from malicious actors
justification: On 3rd of August 2023, Niger’s military blocked local retransmission of the signals of French international news broadcasters Radio France Internationale (RFI) and France 24, violating its public’s right to news and information from varied sources at a time of threats to security in the Sahel.

Since General Abdourahamane Tiani took over in Niger, RSF has seen disturbing signs for the media, including verbal and physical attacks on local and international reporters and calls by junta supporters for Western media to be suspended until further notice.

On 28 July at the headquarters of the Nigerien Party for Democracy and Socialism (PNDS-Tarayya) during a press conference, – the party led by the newly deposed President Mohamed Bazoum – as yet unidentified individuals attacked crews from two privately-owned Nigerien media outlets, the radio network Anfani and the TV channel Bonferey, and damaging a Bonferey camera.

The publisher of Alwihda Info, Djimet Wiché, found himself the target of a car chase as he drove home in the capital, N'Djamena, on the evening of 26 August, when he suddenly realised he was being pursued by two white Toyota Corolla cars with tinted windows. This is the type of car used by Chad’s intelligence agency, the National Security Agency (ANS).

On 25 August, the High Authority for Media and Broadcasting (HAMA) announced that Alwihda Info was suspended from publishing for eight days on the grounds of comments “liable to undermine cohesion and discipline within the army” in two articles. The first, published on 19 August, was about an army colonel’s dismissal by the head of Chad’s military junta, General Mahamat Idriss Déby. The second criticised a speech that the junta chief gave on 20 August.

On October 20, 2022, during the protests against the transitional military government, soldiers stormed into Service Ngardjelaï, a journalist with a pro-government TV channel, at his N’Djamena residence. He found himself face to face with a soldier who slapped him. Despite explaining that he was a Toumai TV journalist, Ngardjelaï was arrested and, with 15 other people. He was tied up in the middle of the yard and severely beaten with sticks and whips.

A reporter for La Voix du Paysan radio in the southern town of Doba, Janvier Mouatangar, was arrested on August 8 by gendarmes and was held overnight after he covered the destruction of 24 fields of crops by nomad-owned cattle.

The Radio Gaya Tcholwa editor Anner Sabartang was arrested by the gendarmerie on the local prefect’s orders on 10 August after he posted a report on WhatsApp about local discontent about the prefect’s decision to appoint a traditional Arab nomad chief to an official position. He was handcuffed and subjected to a long interrogation.

The journalist, Evariste Djaï-Loramadji, who worked at Radio Lotiko, provided a brief live report at 4:39 p.m. on 9 February, in which he said people were “fleeing into the bush” in a confused situation in his village, Sandana, located 600 km southeast of the capital, N’djamena. After this report, he was found in the early evening by a colleague who had arrived from a nearby locality. He had been shot several times in the head.

On 13 February, 21 journalists were arrested by members of the National Intelligence Agency (ANR) during a demonstration in defence of press freedom in Mbandaka. They were held arbitrarily at the ANR’s local headquarters for several hours before being released. They had been demonstrating above all in support of Mimi Etaka, the provincial director of the national radio and TV broadcast RTNC, who had been the victim of a physical attack.

On 5 February, Équateur Governor Bolumbu forced his way into RTNC’s local headquarters accompanied by bodyguards, whom he ordered to beat Etaka for refusing to broadcast three of his decrees appointing new members to his provincial government. Etaka had nonetheless agreed to broadcast the decrees after the news show earlier in the day, albeit without interrupting the show as requested. Despite her attempts to defend herself, the bodyguards tore her clothes off and ransacked RTNC’s premises.

The director of Radio Télévision Sarah (RTS), Steve Mwanyo Iwewe, has been hiding since 29 January, when the Équateur Governor Bolumbu ordered the ARN to arrest him. Iwewe’s offence was to have hosted a broadcast on 27 January in which guests criticised the interior minister’s decision to restore Bolumbu to the governorship following his suspension on 11 January over election fraud allegations. Gunmen tried to break into Iwewe’s house on the night of 16 February, to intimidate him before leaving.

The Équateur Governor Bolumbu had ordered RTS’s closure in November 2021 but a court of appeal declared the closure illegal. In June 2023, when RTS had just been authorised to resume broadcasting after being off the air for 19 months, the provincial justice minister went with police officers to the radio station's premises on the governor’s orders and prevented its journalists from returning to work by denying them entry.

Cholera is blamed on community leaders, who are said believed to be spreading the disease deliberately – whereas, in reality, they are among those promoting the hygiene measures that can stop water-borne diseases such as cholera.

A wave of disinformation about the causes of cholera has led to the murder of at least three community leaders and the destruction of 50 houses in the northern Mozambican province of Cabo Delgado, according to a report in Wednesday’s issue of the independent newssheet “Carta de Mocambique”.

At least 23 people died and another 30 were injured during a wave of cholera disinformation in Mozambique, according to data released in January by PRM General Commander, Bernardino Rafael.

In addition to the dead and injured, 91 mainly government and local authority buildings were vandalised.

The World Health Organization has warned against misinformation of the spread of cholera outbreak. This is coming following the false claims about the spread of a cholera outbreak in northern Mozambique which have led to violent protests and deaths, according to health officials.

The arrest at a Thon Buri condominium on Thursday followed numerous complaints lodged with police via the IDMB Facebook page. Complainants reported that the suspect had persuaded them to invest in a forex trading scheme.

Concerns have arisen about an eight-year-old boy's welfare, as his parents claim he has telepathic abilities that can connect people's minds. They also assert that he was a son of Lord Buddha in a previous life and has acquired the miraculous powers of the naga, a giant serpent in Thai mythology.

Two suspects have been arrested for allegedly defrauding a businessman out of more than 300 million baht through an online cryptocurrency investment scam. They were charged with colluding in public fraud, inputting false information into a computer system, and laundering money, according to Pol Col Adichart Amornpradit of CCIB division 3 on Wednesday.
In just the first week of this year, at least 18 journalists were assaulted while covering alleged election irregularities and violence in Bangladesh.

The acclaimed journalist and human rights defender soon uncovered a banking scandal that has devastated her local community. However, a public figure implicated in the alleged fraud has filed criminal defamation complaints against her, and now she faces up to 18 years in prison. She is just one of tens of thousands who have been charged with criminal defamation in the past decade.

To protect public health amidst heatwave conditions, the Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE) plan has been established with essential information on heatwaves. This plan has been tailored and shared within Rohingya communities following approval from the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS). The dissemination of these messages is being carried out through various methods, including printed posters, door-to-door visits, community awareness sessions, and the involvement of community leaders to ensure widespread awareness.

UNHCR continues its efforts to build the capacities of the organizations and staff working on Bhasan Char. In this regard, three camp coordination and camp management training sessions were delivered to government and humanitarian actors. Seventy-eight NGO and government staff were trained on emergency response, including fire safety and cyclone preparedness and response.

The draft bill, set to replace a 2002 law, suggests limitations on content involving "exclusive investigative journalism," alcohol, depictions of "professions or figures with negative lifestyles," as well as homosexual and transgender behaviors. These restrictions align with the broadcast content standards that the Indonesian Broadcasting Commission (KPI) aims to implement, as per a version of the draft bill acquired by BenarNews.

Early today in Savar, police detained two individuals in connection with the assault on a local correspondent for The Daily Star. The individuals apprehended are Monir Hossen and Babul, according to Sudip Kumar Gope, the sub-inspector of Savar Model Police Station. Previously, on Sunday, Aklakur Rahman Akash, a correspondent for The Daily Star, was brutally attacked while reporting on a conflict between the owners of a ceramic factory in Savar.

A journalist from Islampur upazila in Jamalpur was reportedly stabbed by a local businessman. The Officer-in-Charge of the Police Station reported that Enamul Haque was informed about a significant quantity of VGF rice being stored unlawfully at Asad Dali Rice Mill. Subsequently, Enamul and three other journalists visited the location and entered the mill. An argument ensued between Enamul and the mill owner regarding the VGF rice sacks, the owner stabbed Enamul in the abdomen, critically wounding him.

In November 2023, an online video depicted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in Medina, Saudi Arabia, being welcomed with chants of "Bhua, bhua." However, the authentic footage of the prime minister's visit to Medina contained no such background noise, and it was determined that the audio had been superimposed from a separate, unrelated event.

A Kyi Pan Malun lies within territory controlled by the resistance, approximately 12 kilometers northeast of Kyaukhtu town along the Pakokku road. In the days preceding the airstrike, the area was cut off from internet and phone services. According to the locals, such internet blackouts frequently occur before airstrikes.

The Committee to Protect Journalists has called for the immediate identification and prosecution of individuals responsible for the shooting threats and harassment directed at Rappler reporter Joann Manabat and K5 News FM Olongapo reporter Rowena Quejada. On March 12, men armed and wearing red and white shirts, identified with Clarkhills Properties Corporation, verbally prevented Manabat and Quejada from accessing a disputed land area in Anunas village, Angeles City, Pampanga province.

On the evening of February 28, as many as 15 police officers assaulted Pokhrel, the editor-in-chief of Pranmancha, a news website, while he was recording the alleged forceful displacement of street vendors in Kathmandu's Sundhara area. Pokhrel informed CPJ that the officers seized his phone, camera, and laptop, as well as additional items he had bought earlier that day, totaling approximately 11,000 rupees (US $82).

Journalist Rana was detained for a week following his arrest on March 5. Employed by Desh Rupantor, Rana was apprehended at a government office in the Sherpur district after submitting a right to information request about a government development initiative. Subsequently, an assistant land commissioner, also serving as an executive magistrate, sentenced Rana to a six-month prison term for charges of non-compliance with a public servant's order and for insulting the modesty of a woman.

On March 5, in the evening, Sri Lanka police service's Criminal Investigation Department officers arrested G.P. Nissanka, the owner and editor of Ravana Lanka News, at his residence in Pallebedda, Sabaragamuwa Province. According to Amila Egodamahawatta, Nissanka's attorney, the journalist was detained in police custody until his release on bail on March 20. As of the last update, his mobile phone, confiscated at the time of arrest, was still held by the police, Egodamahawatta reported.

Documentary filmmaker Shin Daewe was detained on October 15, 2023, while collecting a video drone ordered online for documentary filming purposes. After an interrogation lasting nearly two weeks, Shin Daewe faced trial by a secret military tribunal without legal counsel. On January 10, 2024, Shin Daewe received a conviction under Section 50(j) of the Anti-Terrorism Law, which permits life imprisonment for the financing of terrorist acts.

Development Media Group reporter Htet Aung could be jailed for 12 years under two separate charges. He was arrested while taking photos of soldiers making donations to Buddhist monks during a religious festival in the Rakhine State in October.

On Tuesday, May 21, four plainclothes police officers entered the headquarters of Kantipur Media Group (KMG) in Kathmandu, Nepal's capital, and arrested Sirohiya on charges of alleged citizenship irregularities. Recently, KMG outlets had published a series of critical reports, including on Monday and Tuesday, the day of Sirohiya's arrest, accusing Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister Rabi Lamichhane of involvement in the misappropriation of cooperative funds during his tenure as managing director of Gorkha Media Network.

Kaspersky reported that in 2023, its products identified 15 million local incidents on the computers of participants in the Kaspersky Security Network in Sri Lanka. Nearly 46 percent of users in Sri Lanka encountered local threats during this time. Furthermore, Kaspersky detected 9.3 million distinct Internet-borne cyberthreats on the computers of KSN participants in Sri Lanka, with 39.5 percent of users facing web-borne threats in the same period.

The UNFPA is dedicated to placing communities at the forefront of disaster preparedness initiatives in the Philippines. In pursuit of this, dialogues are being held nationwide to gather insights from the varied experiences of women, men, youth, indigenous peoples, LGBTQIA+ members, and other marginalized groups.

subindicator: ILS2.2 - Accessible, safe and accurate information
justification: The Philippines is a country where nearly 9 percent of the population are Indigenous Peoples, and the government fully recognizes IP rights in its constitution and national legislation. Yet determining or analyzing the extent and composition of the country’s IP population has long been difficult, since much of the data collected for official statistics is not disaggregated. Additionally, for the IP-related data that does exist, there is a lack of coherence between the various datasets maintained across the government.

subindicator: ILS2.2 - Accessible, safe and accurate information
justification: Indigenous Peoples (IPs) are nearly invisible in the country’s official public data. This absence of comprehensive data leads to a lack of understanding of IPs’ socio-demographic profiles and the extent of disadvantages they face in the Philippines. Moreover, without proper data, it is nearly impossible to propose accurate poverty reduction strategies or to improve IP targeting for social programs.

subindicator: ILS2.1 - Telecommunications infrastructures damage or limitations
justification: Rainfall and consequent floods that hit northern Armenia, particularly Lori and Tavush Provinces, on 26 May, the number of casualties increased. According to media, at least four people died and 429 people have been evacuated across the affected areas. In addition, hundreds of people experienced power cuts, and almost 17 bridges have been destroyed.
source_name: European Commission's Directorate-General for European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations

subindicator: ILS2.2 - Accessible, safe and accurate information
justification: Refugees frequently express a lack of information regarding employment laws for both employees and employers, compounding the challenges of navigating the employment landscape. As a result, refugees often find themselves restricted to informal sector jobs or self-employment initiative.

subindicator: ILS2.2 - Accessible, safe and accurate information
justification: Some households in West Nile have received start-up capital, empowering women to initiate various home-based businesses aimed at supporting household self-reliance. Moreover, many refugees lack information on the requirements and procedures for registering these businesses.

subindicator: ILS2.1 - Telecommunications infrastructures damage or limitations
justification: The cyclone, Tropical Depression AGHON has intensified into Typhoon EWINIAR, equivalent to a Category 2 hurricane. As a result, 52 cities/municipalities are experiencing interrupted power supply, and 4 have disrupted communication lines.

subindicator: ILS2.2 - Accessible, safe and accurate information
justification: Period poverty is further exacerbated by stigma and a lack of information and education. Many girls and young women are not only unaware and unprepared for menstruation, but also policymakers and those in authority in schools and workplaces lack thorough menstrual education. In Bangladesh, merely 32% of girls, respectively, were informed about menstruation before experiencing their first period, leaving many feeling shocked and frightened.

indicator: ILI3 - Vulnerability of specific groups within the context / safety and dignity of people accessing information
justification: Stigma and discrimination intensify in communities with harmful social and cultural norms surrounding menstruation. Even now, in various regions, menstruating girls and women are perceived as impure or untouchable, which limits their freedom and access to certain spaces. Common myths perpetuate the belief that menstruating individuals should not handle certain foods, lest they spoil, or enter sacred spaces, and that they should be isolated.

subindicator: ILS4.4 - Deliberate communication shutdowns / restrictions from malicious actors
justification: Tom Andrews, the UN Special Rapporteur on the human rights situation in Myanmar, stated that despite the military-imposed internet shutdown making it challenging to get information from Northern Rakhine, alarming and credible reports of killings, enforced disappearances, and widespread arson are emerging.

An independent online reporter was killed by unidentified gunmen outside his home. He ran a YouTube channel and a Facebook TV news channel in which he covered the social problems that his fellow citizens face in North Waziristan. This journalist’s murder highlights the perilous environment in which Pakistani media professionals work. Pakistan continues to be one of the world’s most dangerous countries for journalists

The attacks against reporters have taken place during protests since 19 April. At least five journalists were targeted. Some were pushed to the ground, others beaten and one journalist was even hit by a police vehicle.  As well as sometimes targeted by the police, journalists are also often attacked in the street and by politicians who are supposed to guarantee press freedom

The Special Rapporteur received reports that human rights defenders, students, activists, journalists, opposition politicians, and academics have faced harassment, detention, and in some instances, alleged torture while in custody, leading to deaths. From 2019 to 2023, as many as 2,889 individuals were charged under the Digital Security Act.

Digital Security Act to arrest individuals under a wide range of offences – such as hurting religious sentiments, criticism on the liberation war, spreading misinformation about coronavirus disease (COVID-19), or criticizing the response to it by the Government and others.9 Those accused and placed in detention often had to remain in custody for long periods of time until a bail order could be issued by the higher courts.

Section 32 of the Digital Security Act invokes the Official Secrets Act, which allows for a penalty of up to 14 years in prison or a fine of up to 2,500,000 taka for "violating government confidentiality." This provision has been employed to create an atmosphere of intimidation and censorship, restricting discussions on matters of public concern.

The IRC aims to engage at least 10,000 educators and caregivers in ongoing and immediate crises in regions including Northeast Nigeria, Colombia, and Bangladesh with this initiative, thereby indirectly benefiting over half a million students. Through integration with OpenAI's ChatGPT, the IRC will quickly generate content, assist overburdened teachers, and tailor digital educational experiences to enhance learning results and empower teachers, all while evaluating the impact of AI on education in secure and ethical manners.

justification: Stigma surrounding mental health in Uganda act as a significant barrier for refugees to seeking support from the limited number of mental health services.

justification: Limited access to information about social protection schemes exacerbates vulnerabilities among the population, with participants in FGDs expressing concern that accessing National Social Security Fund (NSSF) benefits could jeopardise their refugee status.

justification: Reports by NRC indicates refugees reported access to comprehensive legal information regarding rights is crucial. Yet, only a limited portion of the community reported possessing such knowledge, with many expressing unawareness of available legal and paralegal services within their communities.

Additionally, instances of delays in follow-up, misconduct,
discrimination, and corruption within law enforcement agencies aggravate these challenges, eroding trust among refugees.

Communications and Information Minister Budi Arie Setiadi has reinitiated a plan to establish a council to monitor social media content and make social media platforms “more accountable”. This move comes despite concerns about its possible effects on online freedom of speech. Discussions regarding the establishment of a "social media council," have reemerged following a series of policy reversals driven by social media, ranging from increased tuition fees and import restrictions to startling disclosures of state corruption and unresolved criminal cases.

Minister of Social Affairs Tri Rismaharini launched the Young Indonesian Economic Heroes (Pena Muda) program to help individuals escape poverty. In a statement from the ministry on Monday, Rismaharini noted that young people aged 20-30 years are prioritized as beneficiaries. Apart from business capital assistance, they will receive support in business development, packaging, marketing, and financial literacy.

Health Minister Budi Gunadi Sadikin said during a working meeting with Commission IX of DPR RI and the Head of the National Population and Family Planning Agency (BKKBN), Hasto Wardoyo, that the Health Ministry is working to improve the accuracy of stunting data across Indonesia. This is being done through training midwives and integrated health post cadres in anthropometric measurement techniques. The training aims to ensure correct measurement using anthropometric tools and is currently ongoing.

According to the 2023 Journalist Safety Index, 45% of 536 surveyed journalists reported experiencing violence in the workplace during 2023. This includes 49% of the 175 female journalists who responded. The most common forms of violence encountered were bans on coverage and reporting, at 46% and 41% respectively.

Himawan stated during a press conference at the National Police headquarters in Jakarta that the syndicate had infiltrated the company's email system to obtain data and critical information related to business transactions. Following this, they established an Indonesian company called PT Huttons Asia Internasional to interact with Kingsford Huray Development.

Malaysian political activist, Badrul Hisham Shaharin, better known as Chegubard, claimed trial to two charges of criminal defamation and sedition at the cybercrime Sessions Court on April 29 since he had allegedly posted comments on Facebook claiming there was a plan to build a casino in Forest City to revive the township. Bloomberg journalist, Ram Anand, has also been called for investigation by the Bukit Aman police for sedition, criminal defamation and the misuse of network facilities.

Pranksters online have been spreading fake news including fake reports against Philippine officials involved in the campaign to protect the WPS. The report mentions that the news stories included a supposed Philippine exposé claiming China’s illegal actions in the WPS would lead to war. Another fake news piece alleged that China’s ‘aggression’ is a result of Philippines’ deepening security activities with the United States, while a third said that Philippines’ actions are dictated by the US, the report added.

On Monday, Malaysia introduced new regulations that critics claim impose stricter content restrictions for local filmmakers, emphasizing that the Film Censorship Board will not tolerate subjects that could disturb the religious and cultural sensitivities of certain individuals. Consequently, Malaysian films featuring discussions on racial tensions, inquiries about religious practices, or LGBTQ characters might face censorship or may not be released at all.
A health expert at the Lainya health center, Justin Duku, attributed the increase in the number of teenage pregnancy to the lack of adolescent health education at homes and in schools.

The county Paramount Chief, Ladu identified one of the causes of the problem -increase of teenage pregnancy as the lack of sensitization of the population, which made many parents not to report their cases to the authorities.

Alpha TV journalist Rena Kouvelioti was seriously injured on 14 May 2024 after being assaulted by a company's operator while reporting on oxygen welding. Kouvelioti was reporting on a construction site in Lagonisi, Attica region in Greece - where welding was being done next to dry grass before a man identified as the company’s operator hit the journalist. Kouveliot described an unexpected attack she faced after inquiring about the authorisation for the work being done at the site.

On 9 April 2024, Jordanian security forces arrested Atia Abu Salem, a Syrian student at Yarmouk University, in the capital, Amman, according to media reports and his lawyer Ahmad Sawai, who spoke to the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ). Abu Salem was arrested along with Jordanian student journalist Abdul Rahman Alsheikh while they were headed to film an evening pro-Palestinian protest in front of the Israeli embassy. Alsheikh was later released, according to Sawai.

Journalist by the name Eze was arrested by police according to reports by Sahara Reporters. The arrest has been a described as continuation of an ongoing assault by the Nigerian police on press freedom.

On 5 June 2024, journalist Makawi Mohamed Ahmed, a reporter at the official state news agency of Sudan (SUNA), and his brother Shamseddine Mohamed Ahmed were killed by the paramilitary group Rapid Support Forces (RSF) during its attack on the village of Wad Al-Noura. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) was unable to confirm further details about Ahmed’s death.
On 4 June 2024, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) shot and killed investigative journalist Muawiya Abdel Razek and three of his family members in his home in Khartoum.

As of May 30 2024 since the beginning of the full-scale invasion of the Russian Federation on the territory of Ukraine at least 91 media workers were killed. According to NSJU and the International Federation of Journalists among the dead are 16 media people who were performing professional duties; 9 media people - civilian victims; 66 representatives of mass media who mobilized for the defense of Ukraine in the ranks of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.

The Royal Malaysian Police (PDRM) has identified the Instagram account ‘Muhammad Imran Suresh’ as a fake account, which claimed to have information about the acid attack on national footballer Faisal Halim. Without revealing further details, Bukit Aman Criminal Investigation Department director Datuk Seri Mohd Shuhaily Mohd Zain stated that they are monitoring developments in the ongoing investigation into the case.

The Nepal Media Society condemned the spread of 'fake news' aimed at defaming media and judiciary members and called for immediate action against those responsible. Chairman Subha Shankar Kandel expressed concern over misinformation following a 'sting operation' video and audio clip posted on the YouTube channel of 'Sidha Kura', formerly aired on the defunct Galaxy Television.

The Mongolian Red Cross Society (MRCS) conducted Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) training for 45 volunteers from 21 provinces at the Youth Training Centre from April 22-24. In collaboration with the National Center of Mental Health and the Ministry of Health, the training aimed to enhance the capacity of mid-level branch (MLB) staff and volunteers to provide MHPSS during emergencies, especially during the Dzud response. Additionally, the training sought to establish MHPSS counseling rooms and hotlines at MLB offices.
source_name: International Federation of Red Cross And Red Crescent Societies

Masud, the Bakshiganj correspondent for the daily Samakal, filed a complaint with local police against four named individuals and five to six unnamed others.

Russian Telegram channels, referring to unnamed Ukrainian media, spread disinformation that the risk of epidemics is increasing in Ukraine due to interruptions in electricity, water supply, increasing unsanitary conditions, and declining quality of medicine.

On 30 March 2024, security forces arrested photojournalist Ahmad Mohsen while he was reporting on demonstrations in front of the Israeli embassy in Amman. Mohsen was wearing a press vest and a press badge. On 1 April 2024, Amman’s governor ordered Mohsen’s administrative detention and he was taken to the city’s Marka prison. On 6 April 2024, Mohsen was moved to Al-Salt prison. The governor refused to release him on bail. Mohsen was released on bail on 19 April 2024.

She now survives on what casual labour she can find as well as support from neighbour

A fake notice circulating on social media claims that the Higher Secondary School exams will be postponed by a month due to the aftermath of Cyclone Remal, causing confusion among students and parents. Mohammad Abul Khair, the public relations officer of the MESHED, confirmed that no such decision has been made. The false notice, which began spreading on Thursday, wrongly stated that the exam dates had been changed due to the cyclone, flooding, and student movements.

justification: For many girls and young women coming out of Boko Haram, returning to their communities and their relatives in IDP camps or towns has not been easy. Meta, Facebook's parent company, has removed numerous accounts and pages associated with Bangladesh’s ruling party, Awami League, due to "coordinated inauthentic behaviour" ahead of the January elections. The announcement was made on Thursday, stating that Facebook took down "50 accounts and 98 pages for violating our policy against coordinated inauthentic behaviour." These accounts were involved in activities such as pretending to be opposition supporters while posting content critical of the political opposition.

Members of the Detective Branch (DB) of Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) have arrested three members of an organized gang involved in manipulating the stock market by spreading false information on social media and online platforms. The arrestees are Amir Hossain (alias Nurnurani, 37), Nurul Haque Harun (52), and Abdul Kaiyum (39). They used secret groups on Facebook, WhatsApp, and Telegram to disseminate misleading information related to the stock market, according to Harun.

Amina, a 30-year-old Rohingya woman residing in a refugee camp in Bashanchar, Noakhali district, Bangladesh, shared her experience of participating in a Female Caregiver’s Session at the Adolescent and Youth Centre. She mentioned that the sessions emphasized the importance of proper menstrual hygiene management, helping her to see menstruation as a natural and manageable part of life rather than something to be ashamed of. With this knowledge, she now feels equipped to guide her 10-year-old daughter.

The UNFPA Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific collaborated with UN Volunteers for the first large-scale Online Volunteering initiative, aiming to recruit volunteers to spread awareness and tackle harmful gender and social norms that lead to child marriage. As part of the #EveryGirlCounts campaign, over 150 Online Volunteers were mobilized, reaching over 100,000 social media users within two weeks. They spread messages advocating for gender equality and girls’ equal right to education.

As the pandemic continued, additional courses were translated, resulting in a total of 11 COVID-19 courses available by December 2021. The course links were disseminated through prominent websites managed by the Ministry of Health (MoH) and the Indonesia Hospital Association (PERSI), extending their reach. In May 2021, WHO launched the "Serving Countries: Indonesia" webpage, which compiles OpenWHO courses in Indonesian, further expanding access to essential knowledge.
