subindicator: ILS2.2 - Accessible, safe and accurate information
justification:
The Ministry of Reintegration of the Temporarily Occupied Territories has opened a round-the-clock hotline for residents of the Kursk region who want to evacuate to Ukraine or need humanitarian assistance.

Context: since approximately August 6 Ukrainian Armed Forces incuse to the territory of Kursk region - Russian region on the border with Sumy region. After almost a week of total informational silence Ukrainian authorities publicly acknowledged the operation and claimed the control of 1000 square kilometres and dozens settlements.

In early 2024, Access Now and the Citizen Lab identified a different cluster of phishing attacks. The organizations and individuals targeted in this campaign included Russian and Belarusian civil society organizations and independent media, international NGOs, and at least one former US ambassador. Citizen Lab has attributed this campaign to a Russia-based threat group COLDRIVER, also possessing other names. According to several governments, this group is a subordinate of the Russian Federal Security Service (FSB)’s Centre 18.

In Russia, by August 2024, more than 10,000 reports were drawn up for anti-war statements. The total amount of fines at the end of 2023 amounted to 227.8 million rubles, and 194 people were brought to criminal responsibility.

subindicator: ILS2.2 - Accessible, safe and accurate information
justification:
The Ukrainian media published the first footage from the Kursk region of the Russian Federation, showing a report from Sudzha. The military told about the mood when entering the territory of the Russian Federation, and journalists showed the life of local residents.

Since approximately August 6 Ukrainian Armed Forces incuse to the territory of Kursk region - Russian region on the border with Sumy region. After almost a week of total informational silence Ukrainian authorities publicly acknowledged the operation.

subindicator: ILS4.4 - Deliberate communication shutdowns / restrictions from malicious actors
justification: The government declared a public holiday from 5 to 7 August, during which mobile internet services were temporarily suspended.

On 31 July 2024, Mohammed Abu Jasser, a Palestinian journalist working for the Hamas-affiliated newspaper Al-Risala and the pro-Hamas newspaper Felesteen, was killed along with his mother, wife, and at least two of his children in an Israeli airstrike at about 3 a.m. in Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza. Abu Jasser was born onSeptember 7, 1985. He obtained a master’s degree in journalism from the Islamic University of Gaza and freelanced for multiple outlets.

On 5 July 2024, Saadi Madoukh, a Palestinian journalist and freelance camera operator for outlets including Al Jazeer and the Turkish state broadcaster TRT, was killed in an Israeli airstrike in the Al Daraj neighborhood in Gaza City, according to news reports, the Palestinian press freedom group MADA, and the International Federation of Journalists. Madoukh was also the founder and CEO of Deep Shot media production company. Adeeb Sukkar, another media worker, was injured in the strike that killed Madoukh.

Mohammed Abu Sharia, managing editor of the local privately owned Shams News Agency, was injured in an Israeli airstrike in the Al-Sabra neighborhood in Gaza City on 29 June 2024, resulting in severe head injuries. He was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit of the Indonesian Hospital and died on 1 July 2024.

Abu Sharia studied journalism and worked for various outlets before becoming a reporter at Shams News Agency, where he was later promoted to managing editor.

On 31 May 2024, Ola Al Dahdouh, a journalist working as an editor and presenter for the local Sawt Al Watan radio station, was killed in an Israeli airstrike on her husband’s family home in Gaza City’s Al Jalaa neighborhood. In a post on her Facebook page, her brother Mohannad said that Ola was killed in the airstrike, which he said happened without any prior alert. Al Dahdouh’s husband, Abdelrahman Helles, and her son, Karam, were wounded in the airstrike.

On 16 May 2024, Mahmoud Juhjouh, a Palestinian photographer who worked for the local Palestine Post Network, was killed along with his wife, children, and mother, in an Israeli airstrike on his home in Sheikh Radwan neighborhood of Gaza City, according to his outlet and media reports. Those reports mentioned that Juhjouh had been displaced several times with his family, and had returned to his house after the Israeli army withdrew from northern Gaza.

On 11 May 2024, Bahaa Okasha, a Palestinian camera operator who worked for the Hamas affiliated Al-Aqsa TV channel, was killed in an Israeli airstrike on his home in Al-Qasasib neighborhood in Jabalia refugee camp, northern Gaza, along with his son Hamza and his wife, according to Al Jazeera, Qatari-funded Al-Araby TV, the privately owned Palestinian Maan News Agency, and the privately owned Lebanese newspaper Annahar.

On 6 May 2024, Mustafa Ayyad, a freelance Palestinian photographer, was killed after he was critically injured by an Israeli airstrike on his home in Azzaytoun neighborhood in northern Gaza, according to multiple media reports. Those sources said that Ayyad suffered injuries to his head, heart, and liver, and was taken to Al-Maamadani hospital where he was pronounced dead. Ayyad worked for Al Jazeera Mubashar and Al Jazeera Net on a freelance basis during the war, according to Al Jazeera.

On 29 2024, Salem Abu Toyour, a Palestinian media worker at the Hamas affiliated Al-Quds Al-Youm TV channel, was killed in an Israeli airstrike on his family home in Nuseirat camp, central Gaza, along with two relatives including his son Ahmed, according to Beirut-based press freedom group SKeyes, the independent Palestinian news agency Wattan, Al Jazeera, and the Palestinian Authority official news agency WAFA.

On 26 April 2024, Ibrahim Mohamad Al-Gharbawi, Palestinian freelance photojournalist, was killed along with his brother, Ayman in an Israeli drone strike in the Hamad neighborhood of Khan Yunis, southern Gaza, when they were filming with a drone according to Beirut based-press freedom group SKeyes, the independent Palestinian news agency Shfa, and the Russian state-owned outlet RT. According to the Palestinian Authority official news agency WAFA, the journalists were buried on April 27, 2024, near Al-Aqsa hospital in Deir al-Balah.

Mohammed Bassam Al Jamal, Palestinian photographer working for the pro-Islamic Jihad news agency Palestine Now, was killed after sustaining critical injuries in an Israeli airstrike on his family home in the Al-Jenenah neighborhood in Rafah, southern Gaza. The airstrike occurred at 11:00 p.m. on 24 April 2024, injuring Al Jamal and killing six of his relatives before Al Jamal succumbed to his critical injuries at 5:00 a.m. the next day.

On 28 March 2024, Mohamed Abu Skheil, a Palestinian media worker who worked as an editor and graphic designer for the local privately owned Shams News Agency, was killed by Israeli bullets when the Israeli army raided the Al-Shifa hospital complex in northern Gaza. His outlet said that Abu Skheil was killed inside the hospital after he took refuge in it following the destruction of his house in an Israeli airstrike at the beginning of the war.

On 25 March 2024, Saher Akram Rayan, a journalist who works for the Palestinian Authority official news agency WAFA, was killed with his son, Anas, in an Israeli strike in the west of Gaza City as they were assisting injured neighbors, according to the Palestinian Authority official news agency WAFA, Middle East Eye, the Beirut-based press freedom group SKeyes, and the International Federation of Journalists.

On 14 February 2024, Ayman Al-Rafati, a Palestinian journalist, writer, and political analyst who wrote for the Hezbollah-affiliated broadcaster Al Mayadeen and appeared regularly on Al Mayadeen and Al Jazeera, was killed along with his brother, sister-in-law, and nephews in an Israeli airstrike on his home at Al Jalaa Street in Gaza City. Al-Rafati, who had a PhD and was on the board of the Center for Regional Studies – Palestine, appeared on Al Jazeera hours before his death.

On 11 February 2024, Yasser Mamdouh El-Fady, a 40-year-old journalist for the Islamic Jihad affiliated Kan’an news agency, was killed by an Israeli sniper at the Nasser Hospital in Khan Yunis, according to multiple media reports, and the Beirut-based press freedom group SKeyes.

A Polish journalist will be tried for espionage and cooperation with a Russian spy who participated in the exchange of former prisoners between Russia and the West. According to the publications, the anonymous journalist and the spy had allegedly two years relationship during his stay in Poland. 
The spy is probably Pavlo Rubtsov that worked as a journalist under the name Pablo Gonzalez firstly in Spain than in Poland, where in February 2022 he was detained with a local journalist.

The administrator of the Telegram channel from Zhytomyr Oblast was informed of the suspicion of facilitating the illegal crossing of the state border by six conscripted citizens of Ukraine.
According to the investigation, the man became the administrator of the Telegram channel, which published information about the organization of illegal crossing of the state border of Ukraine outside checkpoints.

Russian propaganda is spreading a fake that the US authorities can allegedly consider the scenario of removing the President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky against the background of the operation of the invasion of the Armed Forces of the Kursk region. This thesis of ex-CIA employee Larry Johnson is promoted by the Kremlin media.
What is mentioned is an informational enhance of recent "disclosure" of Russian Foreign Intelligence Service with comments of so-called experts with US citizenship.

In the occupied Crimea, including in Sevastopol, as well as in the temporarily occupied part of the Kherson region, the Russian military intensified propaganda of mobilization to the Russian army, using "all possible methods."
The means are banners, figures of soldiers in shops, even advertisements in the newspaper "Nova Kakhovka".

The Federal Security Service of Russia opened a criminal case against two Italian journalists. They are accused of illegally crossing the border for covering the situation in Suja, Kursk region. The reporters were recalled to Italy for their safety.
Before that, the journalist and cameraman were also threatened with violence by pro-Russian military bloggers.

On September 15, 2022, supporters of the opposition politician Martin Fayulu, president of the Engagement for Citizenship and Development (Ecidé) political party, attacked Tatiana Osango, a reporter with the privately owned YouTube-based news channel Réaco News, on her breasts and other parts of her body and threatened her with rape and death, according to the journalist, who spoke to CPJ via messaging app.

At around 11 a.m. on September 18, 2022, four police officers punched, slapped, and used a belt to hit Didier Kiku and Tésor Bazola, a reporter and a camera operator with the privately owned Tokomi Wapi broadcaster, as they covered demonstrations over the appointment of a new pastor to Kinshasa religious group Evangelical Free Church Africa, according to media reports and the two journalists, who spoke to CPJ by phone.

On September 6 and 7, 2022, armed men dressed in Congolese military uniforms forced their way into the houses of Parfait Katoto, director of privately owned community radio station Amkeni Biakato in the Ituri province, and Picard Luhavo, a reporter with privately owned radio stations, The Voice of Ituri and Mont Bleu, and privately owned news website Monde 24 based in Kinshasa. The armed men threatened the journalists with death, beat them, and confiscated their work equipment.

On the morning of September 8, 2022, Ngoyi, a reporter with the privately owned news site legende.cd, was filming children and blind adults who were begging in the street in Kinshasa, the capital, when some civilians started punching the journalist and accused him of denigrating them by publishing their images online. Shortly after, two plainclothes intelligence agents and a police officer arrested Ngoyi, confiscated the phone he used to film, and detained him for five hours.

On Monday, August 29, 2022, the DRC national police officers arrested Jojo Jibikilayi, a reporter with the privately owned Journal de la Ville news agency, while he covered a protest in Kinshasa, the capital, the journalist told CPJ by phone and messaging app. Jibikilayi was released unconditionally later that day after his lawyer intervened.

On Monday, August 29, 2022, the national officers arrested reporter Emmanuel Tujibikila and camera operator Achède Milantesa, both with the privately owned Pas de Complexe news agency, as they covered the same protest. Tujibikila and Milantesa said they spent a night in detention but were released unconditionally on August 30, after Kinshasa provincial police commissioner General Sylvano Kasongo ordered their release.

On Friday, August 12, officers with the national police arrested and detained for several hours Dimanche Kamate, editor-in-chief of the privately owned Radio Muungano broadcaster in the city of Oicha, in North Kivu province. The officers did not present him with an arrest warrant and at the police station, questioned him about an August 7 broadcast that included guests from Véranda Mutsanga, a local social advocacy group.

On July 28, 2022, a group of police officers at a court in Kinshasa, the capital, attacked and seized two phones belonging to Aloterembi, a reporter with the privately owned Mediacongo.net news website, and threatened him with arrest. Aloterembi was covering a hearing involving opposition politician Jean-Marc Kabund when officers chased and punched him, stopped him for around five minutes on the street, and then let him go after seizing his phones and the equivalent of US$3 in cash.

On July 29, Congolese police forced their way into the office of the privately owned broadcaster Blessing FM in Goma, in North Kivu province, in search of Pacifique Mahamba, a reporter for the station, according to the Observatory of Press Freedom in Africa (OLPA) and Mahamba, who spoke to CPJ in a phone interview.  Pacifique Mahamba said he has been in hiding but planned to go to the Goma police station on Tuesday, August 9, to answer questions.

On August 4, 2022, a person identifying himself as a “general” with the Patriotic Force and Integrationist of Congo (FPIC) armed group sent a message to Jean Christian Bafwa Kabaseke, a reporter and editor with the privately owned broadcaster Candip FM in the northeastern province of Ituri, threatening him over his recent coverage of the group, according to news reports and Bafwa, who spoke to Committee to Protect Journalists in a phone interview.

On the morning of July 5, 2022, a group of six soldiers with the M23 rebel group detained Henry Hererimana Serushago, a reporter at La Voix de Mikeno (RACOM) community radio broadcaster. Serushago told CPJ that he refused to speak to an M23 colonel about the rebel group’s offer to cooperate with RACOM. The colonel then ordered Serushago to be detained, and soldiers forced him to the ground, tied him up, and whipped, kicked, and beat him.

On July 13, 2022, officers with the National Intelligence Agency (ANR) arrested U.S. freelance journalist Nicolas Niarchos and Joseph Kazadi, a Congolese journalist known for his reporting on the mining sector for various local outlets, in the southeastern city of Lubumbashi, and transferred them on July 14 to Kinshasa. Niarchos was released on the night of Monday, July 18, but Kazadi, remained in detention as of Wednesday evening, according to Niarchos’ statement, who spoke to CPJ over the phone.

Through the Accelerating Progress towards Rural Women’s Economic Empowerment (RWEE) project in Madhesh Province, WFP supported 242 smallholder farmers. This initiative provided them with crucial information on weather conditions, agro-advisory services, and market systems. The training also focused on improving their access to financial and business development services, Information and Communication Technology, and other vital resources.

The Security Service of Ukraine reported suspicion to two administrators of Viber channels, who, according to the investigation, helped the men avoid mobilization in Transcarpathia.
"Participants of the channel "merged" current locations of delivery of summonses to conscripts. The channel had more than 500 subscribers, mostly local residents. Another man was exposed in July. The suspect reported the whereabouts of Territorial centers of procurement and social support employees," said spokeswoman of the SSU in Transcarpathia, Wanda Milio.

indicator: ILI3 - Vulnerability of specific groups within the context / safety and dignity of people accessing information
justification:
A 57-year-old resident of Kharkiv Oblast, who humiliated Ukrainian fighters and supported Russian aggression against Ukraine on pro-Russian Internet platforms, will appear before the court. 
"In the Telegram messenger, the man joined pro-Russian groups, where he actively commented on propaganda posts. Also, in his comments on the Kremlin sites, the man called servicemen of the Armed Forces of Ukraine "terrorists" and other offensive words...", the message reads.

A 57-year-old resident of Kharkiv Oblast, who humiliated Ukrainian fighters and supported Russian aggression against Ukraine on pro-Russian Internet platforms, will appear before the court. 
"In the Telegram messenger, the man joined pro-Russian groups, where he actively commented on propaganda posts. Also, in his comments on the Kremlin sites, the man called servicemen of the Armed Forces of Ukraine "terrorists" and other offensive words...", the message reads.

The Security Service of Ukraine in Zhytomyr region exposed an alleged supporter of the USSR, who was spreading communist propaganda online and supporting the "Russian peace". He publicly justified Russia's armed aggression against Ukraine.
"The suspect took destructive content from the leading Russian media, which are "mouthpieces of the Kremlin", as well as from pro-Russian groups in "Odnoklasnyki" banned in Ukraine, such as "I want to the USSR", "Back in the USSR" and alike...", regional SSU spokeswoman Iryna Martyniuk reported.

The Security Service of Ukraine in Zhytomyr region exposed an alleged supporter of the USSR, who was spreading communist propaganda online and supporting the "Russian peace". He publicly justified Russia's armed aggression against Ukraine.
"The suspect took destructive content from the leading Russian media, which are "mouthpieces of the Kremlin", as well as from pro-Russian groups in "Odnoklasnyki" banned in Ukraine, such as "I want to the USSR", "Back in the USSR" and alike...", regional SSU spokeswoman Iryna Martyniuk reported.

On Tuesday, July 5, 2022, a judge at the High Court in Mbandaka, the capital of the DRC’s western Équateur province, acquitted and released journalist Chilassy Bofumbo, who had been jailed since he covered a November 2021 protest, according to the journalist, who spoke to CPJ by messaging app. Two other journalists — Patrick Lola and Christian Bofaya — remain jailed in the central prison of Mbandaka, according to their lawyer, Pontife Ikolombe, who spoke to CPJ by phone.

The government computer emergency response team CERT-UA recorded e-mails cyber attacks with the subject of prisoners of war from the Kursk region of the Russian Federation. It`s noted that letters contain photos of alleged prisoners of war and a link to download the "spysok_kursk.zip" archive. There`s a file with the extension CHM and name "list of POWs that are eliminated. Kursk."

Opening will download SPECTR spyware components to your computer, and FIRMACHAGENT, which is designed to upload stolen data to server.

From May 30, 2022, Stanis Bujakera, a reporter with privately owned, France-based Jeune Afrique news site, Reuters, and Congolese online outlet actualité.cd, John Lungila, a reporter with local, privately owned Educ TV broadcaster, and Steve Wembi, a freelance reporter, have repeatedly received threats, including of death and insults via social media and telephone calls accusing them of supporting Rwanda concerning the conflict in the DRC’s east, they told CPJ in interviews via messaging app and phone.

On May 18, Freddy Sombo, the head of the National Intelligence Agency in the province of Tshuapa, summoned Cédar Sabiti, Samuel Matela, and Junior Batu Ngole, reporters of privately owned Radio stations. When the journalists arrived, Sombo yelled at them and accused them of tarnishing ANR’s image during a May 17 radio program. Sombo then ordered his agents to strip the journalists and lock them in the ANR jail cells, where six officers beat the journalists with truncheons.

On January 10, Bobo Boloko Bolumbu, the governor of Equateur province, ordered the arrest of Patrick Lola, a freelance reporter and Christian Bofaya, a reporter for the privately owned E Radio. According to news reports, Lola and Bofaya were covering a public protest organized by three provincial deputies whose election had been invalidated by the provincial assembly in October 2021. Police arrested the journalists and the three deputies for allegedly disturbing public order.

On April 22, officers with the Congolese National Police Mobile Intervention Group arrested Albert Muhila, Dieu Agba, and Patrick Gbondo, who work as reporters and presenters with the privately owned broadcaster Radio Mwana Mboka, at the station’s office in the northwestern town of Bumba. Police said the journalists were detained concerning a criminal insult complaint over an April 20 broadcast in which they all appeared, Dieu Agba told CPJ.

At around 3 a.m. on April 21, police arrested Mulamba, a journalist and director of the privately owned Kisangani News, at his home in Kisangani, the capital of the northern Tshopo province, according to press reports. The officers then took Mulamba to the local police station held him for six hours, and later released him with his phone and charged him with illegal possession of weapons, criminal association, and armed robbery.

The Gambian police officers arrested Bakary Mankajang on Wednesday, September 20, after he responded to a police summons at Faji Kunda police station outside the capital, Banjul. Mankajang recently travelled to Casamance to conduct interviews about the killings of police officers.

On May 31, 2023, four security guards working for Gambia’s ruling National People’s Party grabbed, repeatedly punched, and poured water on Malick D. Cham, a presenter with the online broadcaster Jamano Media and Products, after the journalist tried to film an NPP politician and another man arguing at a mayor’s swearing-in ceremony in the capital city of Banjul.

The director of the Facebook news page YBC-Communication, Yeri Bocoum, was last seen by his family outside his home in Kati, a district in the western region of Koulikoro, on the afternoon of June 8, according to a statement by his outlet and a person familiar with the case who spoke to CPJ. The day before Bocoum disappeared, he covered a banned demonstration by the opposition political group in Bamako, the capital.

On Thursday, the country’s High Authority for Communication (HAC) issued a directive that “invited all media” to “stop all broadcasting and publication” of coverage of political parties and activities of a political nature of associations, according to the HAC press release and news reports.
The State Tax Service of Ukraine reported on the mass distribution of e-mails with malicious content allegedly on its behalf.

On the evening of August 16, a large DDOS attack was carried out on monobank(Ukrainian first online bank without traditional branches). On the third day of the cyberattack, the financial institution recorded more than 5.5 billion malicious requests. Later, the attack stopped.
"In just three days, we received more than 7.5 billion requests for our services...", - reported the bank director Oleh Grohovskyi.

In Sumy region, activities of administrators of two groups in one of the messengers were terminated. According to the investigation, since the beginning of the introduction of martial law in Ukraine, the suspects created communities in one of the messengers, where they published messages about the places of mobilization events in the territory of the city of Romny and Romny district.

The women systematically updated information for those who intended to evade mobilization.

Crimean citizen journalist Iryna Danylovych, who was sentenced to 6 years and 11 months in prison by the Russian government in Crimea, is being attacked by lynxes due to the lack of treatment in the Russian colony.

subindicator: ILS4.4 - Deliberate communication shutdowns / restrictions from malicious actors
justification: Communication with people living on the left bank of the Kherson region is happening, but it has become much more difficult. The Russian forces increased filtering measures and pressure on local residents.

subindicator: ILS4.4 - Deliberate communication shutdowns / restrictions from malicious actors
justification: In Khmelnytska oblast, the Security Service of Ukraine blocked Viber and Telegram channels, which, according to the investigation, helped men of draft age avoid mobilization. The resources were "informed" about the activities carried out by the Territorial centers of recruitment and social support in the region.

Woman was sentenced to three years in prison for anti-Ukrainian posts on social networks. The convict is a 63-year-old employee of one of the local enterprises.
"During 2022-2023, a woman on her own page in the banned Odnoklassniki social network distributed Kremlin propaganda materials about the need to join the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine to the Russian Federation and restore the Soviet Union..." the report says.

indicator: ILI3 - Vulnerability of specific groups within the context / safety and dignity of people accessing information
justification: Pensioner was sentenced to three years in prison for anti-Ukrainian posts on banned social networks. After full-scale invasion of the Russian Federation into Ukraine, she called for "death to Bandera people,"(allegedly admirers of Stepan Bandera - Ukrainian far-right leader of the radical militant wing of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists, who is highly controversial and is used in aims of Russian propaganda), admired USSR ''leaders'', compared the "historical" figures of Stalin and Shoigu(formerly Russian Minister of Defence)," the report says.

indicator: ILI3 - Vulnerability of specific groups within the context / safety and dignity of people accessing information
justification: Activists drew attention that headliners of the event planned in Kyiv are Russian-singing artists among them Kharkiv rap group which publicly use banned in Ukraine network Vkontakte and pay taxes to Russia through its service Yandex.Music. They urged organizers to cancel the event, it is mentioned that it not the first time these organizers are dealing with language concerning their events critique.

The Verkhovna Rada registered a government draft law "On Amendments to the Law of Ukraine "On Sanctions" Regarding the Prohibition of the Use of Software Products and Access to Electronic Information Resources", which proposes to ban in Ukraine electronic sites developed by foreign sanctioned persons.
Document mentions in particular prohibitions of legal entities to distribute and use software products or their components originating from a foreign sanctioned state; of the use of software products by entities that carry out terrorist activities.

Belarusian president Aleksander Lukashenko said that Belarus has moved almost a third of its army to the border with Ukraine. This is due to the fact that more than 120,000 soldiers of the Armed Forces of Ukraine are allegedly stationed there.

At the same time, the spokesman of the State Border Service of Ukraine, Andriy Demchenko, said that the situation on the border with Belarus has not changed. Ukrainian border guards did not record the movement of equipment and troops.

In Latvia, famous athlete interrogated by special services because of joke about Russian citizenship.
The Latvian Security Service reviewed the case but found no signs of a criminal act. A conversation was held with former boxing champion Nikita Smirnov, and he was warned of possible criminal liability in case of criminal acts.
Agency noted that such public statements in context of Russia's war against Ukraine don`t meet the interests of national security and create the impression of indirect support for Russian aggression.

On November 7, the attackers fired on the journalists’ vehicle between the eastern town of Ansongo and the city of Gao, where the four planned to attend a journalism training about identifying false information Abdoul Aziz Djibrilla, a presenter with Radio Naata, was killed; Harouna Attino, a news presenter on the Ansongo-based community radio was wounded; and Assaleh Ag Joudou, director of Ansongo-based Radio, and Moustapha Koné, a host at Radio Coton, were kidnapped.

On October 19, police in Bamako, Mali’s capital, summoned Abdoul Niang, director of the privately-owned Malian radio station Émergence FM and an online columnist, to a police station and arrested him. The same day a prosecutor with the cybercrime unit at a local court charged Niang with making false statements likely to disturb public order under the country’s press law, a charge punishable by up to six months in prison and a fine up to 150,000 West African francs.

The Niamey judicial police arrested Idrissa Soumana Maïga four days earlier, on April 25, 2024, and questioned him about a L’Enquêteur article published the same day about allegations that Russian agents placed listening devices in public buildings. An investigative judge at the court in Niamey, the capital, charged Maïga with “undermining national defense” and ordered his transfer to Niamey prison on April 29, 2024.

On Saturday, September 30, 2023, four men in plainclothes arrested Sabou, who regularly posts news and commentary on her Facebook page, at her mother’s home in Niamey, the capital, according to news reports and Abdoul Kader Nouhou, Sabou’s husband, who spoke to CPJ over the phone. The men took Sabou to an unmarked vehicle and placed a hood over her head, then returned to the house and took her phone before driving away.

On July 28, 2023, three masked men in a pickup truck threatened to kidnap Sahiana Maman Hassan, editor of the news magazine Le Témoin de l’Histoire, in Niamey, Niger’s capital. Hassane told CPJ that the masked men stopped him while he was walking near his home, identified him by name, gave his exact address, and threatened to raid his house “very soon” and kidnap him, adding that he “won’t know what happens next.”

On February 9, 2024, security forces sought to quell protests over the postponement of the presidential election until December 15, CPJ documented at least six incidents in the capital, Dakar, in which at least 20 journalists were physically attacked, briefly detained, targeted with tear gas, or harassed in other ways by police.

On February 9, 2024, police officers grabbed Absa Hane, a reporter with the privately-owned Seneweb news website, then slapped and kicked her until she briefly lost consciousness while detaining her for about 30 minutes in a police vehicle, Hane and Mor Amar, a reporter with the privately-owned EnQuête newspaper, told the Committee to Protect Journalists.

On February 9, 2024, Mor Amar, a reporter with the privately-owned EnQuête newspaper, said that another officer also hit him with his fist and repeatedly insulted him at the same time, as seen in a video recorded by a third reporter. The journalists said they were leaving the area as instructed by the police when the officers threw tear gas at them.

On February 9, 2024, a French freelance journalist Thomas Dietrich posted a video on social media and told CPJ that a police officer threw a tear gas canister within “inches” of his face after ordering him to leave a protest.

On February 9, 2024, a police officer threw a tear gas canister toward at least five journalists standing in a street, one of those journalists, Fana Cissé, told CPJ. A video published by the privately-owned news website PressAfrik, where Cissé works as a reporter, shows the officer approaching the journalists, throwing the canister, and the journalists running for cover when it explodes.

On February 9, 2024, Isabelle Bampoky, a reporter for the privately-owned news website Adtv, told the Committee to Protect Journalists that police officers threw a tear gas canister toward the group of journalists she was with, and it exploded near her foot. A video shared on social media showed her being helped to walk after she had inhaled the tear gas.

On February 9, 2024, police targeted Sadikh Diop, a cameraperson for the privately-owned news website Senegal 7, with a tear gas canister while he filmed a convoy of police pickup trucks, another Senegal 7 reporter, Matar Cissé, told the Committee to Protect Journalists. A video Diop shot of the incident shows the convoy and Diop talking, then him screaming after the canister explodes.

On February 9, 2024, El Hadj Mané, a cameraperson for the privately-owned online television channel Flash Info, and Senegal 7 cameraperson Amidou Sall told CPJ that police fired tear gas towards them and a group of at least eight other journalists conducting an interview near a protest.

On February 5, 2024, police officers ordered Ngoné Diop, a reporter for the privately-owned news website Sans Limites to move away as she covered the arrest of an opposition parliamentarian for participating in a banned rally. Ngoné Diop moved from her location, but police threw a tear gas canister in her direction and then, after she went to a nearby rooftop to continue coverage, an officer followed her, ordered her to move again, and prevented her from filming.

subindicator: ILS4.4 - Deliberate communication shutdowns / restrictions from malicious actors
justification: On February 4, 2024, Senegal’s Ministry of Communication, Telecommunications, and Digital Economy (MCTPEN) announced it had “temporarily” suspended access to mobile internet due to “hateful and subversive” messages on social media, without indicating the duration of the cutoff. Internet users began to notice disruption to their mobile connectivity on Monday, according to CPJ’s review of service in the country.

On February 4, 2024, Senegalese authorities permanently withdrew the broadcasting license of Walf TV, the television broadcast service of the privately owned media group Wal Fadjri and one of the country’s major broadcasters, according to CPJ’s review of access to the channel in the country and a copy of the MCTPEN’s decision.

On February 4, 2024, officers with Senegal’s gendarmerie in Dakar, the capital, harassed and briefly detained reporters Sokhna Ndack Mbacké, with the privately owned online news site Agora TV, and Khadija Ndate Diouf, with the privately owned television channel Itv, before releasing them without charge. Mbacké told CPJ, that the officers snatched her phone and insulted both of them, and one officer threatened her with imprisonment if he saw her again.

On February 4, 2024, a different group of gendarmerie officers harassed Hadiya Talla, editor-in-chief of the privately owned news site La Vallée Info, interrupting his live broadcast from the protests in Dakar, according to Talla, who spoke to the Committee to Protect Journalists. An officer grabbed Talla’s phone and insulted him before returning it, and then later another officer interrupted his live coverage and ordered him to stop reporting, before letting Talla continue.

On February 4, 2024, a group of gendarmes twice threw tear gas in the direction of Clément Bonnerot, a correspondent for the French-language global broadcaster TV5 Monde, as he stood alone in a Dakar street, filming the security forces, according to Bonnerot and CPJ’s review of a video he shared of the scene. Bonnerot told CPJ that another gendarme later accused him of “following him” and warned not to “provoke him.”

On November 17, 2023, a Dakar court charged four of the journalists—news presenter Ndèye Astou Bâ, columnist Papa El Hadji Omar Yally, camera operator Daouda Sow, and manager Maniane Sène Lô—with defamation, public insults, and usurpation of the position of a journalist according to the same colleague and their lawyer, Famara Faty, who spoke to Committee to Protect Journalists.

On November 13, 2023, Pape Sané was arrested by officers with the Colobane research section of the gendarmerie as he left the privately owned Walfadjri press group’s offices in Dakar, Senegal’s capital, according to Moustapha Diop, Walfadjri’s radio and television director.

On August 15, 2023, Police summoned Sakho, a reporter with the privately owned Senego news website, to the Division of Criminal Investigations in the capital, Dakar, on Tuesday, according to the outlet’s editor-in-chief, Mangoné Ka both spoke to CPJ by phone. Mangoné Ka told CPJ that the police also summoned him on Monday, and questioned about an article published Sunday, August 13, about alleged secret negotiations for the release of opposition politician Ousmane Sonko.

On June 1, 2023, Senegalese Minister of Communication, Telecommunications, and Digital Economy Moussa Bocar Thiam ordered a 30-day suspension of Walf TV, the television broadcast service of the privately owned media group Wal Fadjri, over its coverage of ongoing countrywide protests.
32 Ukrainian journalists are being held captive in Russia, and negotiations are underway for their immediate release, the acting Minister of Culture and Information Policy said.

Russian authorities in NGCAs have extended the term of "Russian world" program, which provides equipment to receive a pool of Russian propaganda channels.
Residents of the NGCAs aren`t willing to take these kits, which had been issuing for free since 2022. Russian authorities in NGCAs were forced to issued them upon receipt of Russian documents.

Only those admin units which aren`t under the control of Ukrainian government to huge extent since 2022 including(some parts of Donetsk and Luhansk regions - since 2014).

On March 3, 2023, the police in the capital city of Dakar detained Ndiaye after he responded to a summons, according to media reports and the journalist’s lawyer Moussa Sarr, who spoke to the Committee to Protect Journalists by phone and messaging app.

On April 15, 2024, police officers with covered faces arrested Thomas Dietrich and seized his phone as he left the HAAC, according to the journalist. After searching his hotel room, police took Dietrich to an unnamed building where they forcibly removed his wedding ring, slapped, stripped and accused him of “speaking badly about the president,” said Dietrich, adding that his ring and phone were returned by police the following day.

On March 26, the Research and Investigation Brigade (BRI), a division of the Togolese National Police, summoned and detained Mewenemesse at its office in Lomé following a judicial inquiry requested by Mawame Talaka, the public prosecutor at the Lomé court, Talaka told the Committee to Protect Journalists.

On March 4, 2024, Togo’s media regulator, the High Authority for Audiovisual and Communication (HAAC) suspended the privately owned La Dépêche for three months over its February 28 report that questioned the 2023 conviction of Major General Abalo Kadangha for the murder of Lieutenant-Colonel Bitala Madjoulba in 2020, according to the newspaper’s editor Apollinaire Mewenemesse.

On November 14, 2023, an investigating judge at a Lomé court charged Lawson, publication director of the privately-owned newspaper Le Flambeau des Démocrates, and Sossou, a freelance reporter, with disseminating false news and attacking the honor of a minister. The journalists were arrested following a complaint by Togo’s Minister of Urban Planning and Land Reform, Kodjo Sévon-Tépé Adédzé, over posts by the journalists on social media discussing the alleged theft of money from Adédzé’s home.

On April 30, 2023, Togolese soldiers arrested Edouard Kamboissoa Samboee, the founder and owner of the privately owned Laabali news website, as he was reporting on the aftermath of a jihadist attack in Togo’s northern Waldjouaque village, according to the journalist and Robert Douti, Laabali’s editorial director, who both spoke to the Committee to Protect Journalists by phone.

The court considered the apology to be insincere because of the damage caused by the September 21 article, according to Médard Amétépé, adding that the court then suspended the outlet for three months and fined each of the three defendants —  Liberté, Amétépé, and Afangnowou — four million West African francs (US$5,928) each. The suspension and fine related to an article that alleged a security officer in the Togolese Prime Minister's convoy shot and killed a young man.

On August 31, police officers in Benin’s northwestern Pendjari National Park arrested and detained Ayeni, an editor with the privately owned Foundation for Investigative Journalism, as he was taking pictures at the park for his reporting on environmental conservation. The officers accused Ayeni of involvement with a jihadist terror movement and held him at the police station in the northern city of Parakou, until September 5, when they moved the journalist to Cotonou, Benin’s largest city.

On December 19, 2023, an officer with the police criminal brigade called Virgile Ahouansè, news director of the privately owned internet radio station Crystal News, and asked him to appear the following day at a police station in Porto-Novo, the capital, according to news reports and the journalist, who spoke to CPJ by phone. When Ahouansè arrived at the station on December 20, officers arrested him and held him for 48 hours.

A cholera outbreak-related disinformation led to the deaths of nearly 100 people when an overcrowded makeshift ferry sank off Mozambique, resulting in the drowning of 96 people, many children, and leaving 26 missing.

The Mozambican chapter of the regional press freedom body, MISA, declared that fighting against disinformation is crucial for saving lives, referring to the tragic incident of 98 people drowning when their boat capsized off Mozambique Island in Nampula province.

A wave of disinformation about cholera causes has resulted in the murder of three community leaders and the destruction of 50 houses in the northern Mozambican province of Cabo Delgado, with 14 incidents occurring in five districts of Cabo Delgado.

Dr. T. A. Mavetera, the Hon Minister of ICT, Postal and Courier Services, highlighted the strategic partnership between the Zimbabwean government and the ICDL Foundation, aiming to enhance digital literacy among civil servants and ordinary Zimbabweans through ICDL certification.

Zimbabwe is launching a Digital Ambassadors program to improve tech understanding across the country. Hon Tatenda Mavetera, Zimbabwe's minister of information communication technology, postal and courier services, announced the initiative during a recent ICDL certification event for school teachers. The program aims to empower volunteers to champion digital literacy in their communities, emphasizing the strategic partnership between the government and the ICDL Foundation.

A study by the Postal and Telecommunications Regulatory Authority of Zimbabwe (POTRAZ) and the Research Council of Zimbabwe (RCZ) reveals that Zimbabwe's secondary school teachers have intermediate digital literacy, comparable to developed countries like Spain and Macedonia. The findings highlight Zimbabwe's progress in ICT integration in education, but recommend further improvements in digital infrastructure and training.

Zimbabwe is launching a Digital Ambassadors program to promote digital literacy among its communities. The initiative was announced by Tatenda Mavetera, Zimbabwe's minister of information communication technology, postal and courier services, during a recent International Computer Driving Licence (ICDL) certification event for school teachers.

The Zimbabwean government has enhanced education equity and digital literacy by connecting 3,425 schools to the internet, aiming to improve e-learning opportunities and foster digital competency in urban and rural areas.

Zimbabwe has experienced several government website hacks, including the Ministry of Defence, National University of Science and Technology, and Zoom meetings. While security questions and answers are required for account setup, there is a need for more efforts to promote a cybersecurity culture for both institutions and individuals.

The Zimbabwe National Statistics Agency and the Postal and Telecommunications Regulatory Authority of Zimbabwe reported in September 2021 that 58.8% of Zimbabwean households have a smart phone, with most owners residing in urban areas, highlighting the limited access to smartphones and the continued exclusion of rural and marginalized communities in Zimbabwe.

At a recent graduation ceremony at Solusi University, Zimbabwean computer graduates were urged to drive digital innovation and bridge the digital divide. The event emphasized the need to equip educators with computer network design and deployment skills, aligning with Zimbabwe's Education 5.0 framework, and to promote digital inclusivity and prepare for a future-oriented digital economy.

Zimbabwe's internet penetration rate has risen from 60.6% in 2019 to 73.3% as of December 31, 2023, according to Never Ncube, Chief Executive Officer for Dandemutande, an ICT solution provider in Zimbabwe, during a presentation at a POTRAZ stakeholders engagement indaba focusing on price transparency and service quality.

The Zimbabwean government is launching a Digital Ambassadors Program to promote digital literacy nationwide. The initiative, announced by ICT Minister Tatenda Mavetera, will assign local champions to promote digital literacy within their communities, aiming to bridge the digital divide and enable Zimbabweans to fully participate in the digital economy.

Zimbabwe is facing a significant issue of artistic piracy, causing significant financial losses for local artists. The rise in illegal copying and distribution of music, films, and other creative content is urging the government and industry stakeholders to take stronger action.

MULTICHOICE Zimbabwe general manager Siyabulela Jemsana emphasized that illegal copying and sharing of content, including movies and TV shows, from torrent sites is threatening millions of livelihoods and undermining the future of the creative industry worldwide, ahead of an anti-piracy workshop in Harare.

Mozambique's Minister of Transport and Communications, Mateus Magala, has acknowledged the country's ineffectiveness in combating cyber crime during a speech at the Mozambican technology fair (MOZTECH) under the theme "Cybersecurity-Challenges of Digital Transformation." Magala's remarks were made during the opening of the fair.

In the first half of 2024, the INSA reported 4,623 cyber-attacks targeting public and private institutions, with 98.56 percent successfully thwarted. The volume of attacks was higher than the previous year, reaching 115%. If all attacks were successful, the loss could be over 10.5 billion Birr.

The Commercial Bank of Ethiopia (CBE) has successfully foiled nearly 28,000 cyber-attack attempts since 2022, despite being a primary target for economic and political attacks. However, the recent incident, causing customers to withdraw large amounts of cash and digitally transfer millions, was caused by an internal system glitch.

The May 2024 Index reveals significant differences in cybersecurity risk levels across African countries. Egypt ranked highest, followed by Namibia and South Africa. Ethiopia and Zimbabwe had the highest risks. Other African countries, including Angola, Maldives, Kenya, Ghana, Mauritius, Morocco, Uganda, and Nigeria, continue to face cybersecurity challenges.

The Namibian government reported 2.7 million cyber attacks in 2022, with 7,000 daily attacks, highlighting the need for stronger cyberspace and online platforms, as revealed at the first Namibia International Cybersecurity Conference and Exhibition.

Last Friday, David Tobing, leading the Indonesian Consumer Community (KKI), initiated a lawsuit against the minister. The lawsuit contends that the minister was negligent in preventing and mitigating the consequences of the ransomware attack on the data centre in Surabaya, East Java, on June 20, which caused significant disruptions to hundreds of government databases.

In 2023, ransomware and extortion activities resurged, causing a shift from stable loss trends. Hackers exploited IT and physical supply chain vulnerabilities, targeting businesses of all sizes. This highlights the importance of cyber risk management, consistently ranked as a top concern.

The BoT's circular reveals that Tanzanian banks have suffered significant cyber threats, with 4.89 billion Shillings stolen through mobile and internet banking and Sh. 741 million losses incurred through ATM card skimming.

The Mozambican Minister of Transport and Communications, Mateus Magala, stated that 73% of the population lacks internet access. He emphasized the need for innovative, environmentally friendly solutions involving the private sector to provide internet to all, highlighting the need for a paradigm shift.

In 2023, Ethiopia's internet usage reached 36 million, but only 35% of the population is online. Digital IDs and mobile payments are paving the way for a thriving digital ecosystem, while Ethiopia's high mobile phone penetration rate of over 40 million accounts demonstrates potential for digital inclusion.

subindicator: ILS2.2 - Accessible, safe and accurate information
justification: Community dialogues were held in Adjumani, Kyegegwa, and Kikube, reaching 13,399 community members (5,937 male and 7,462 female) with messages on social norm change, GBV risk mitigation, and VAC prevention.

The digital divide in Ethiopia is widening, with many lacking the necessary skills to navigate the online world, limiting their access to digital growth, despite improved connectivity in major cities.

The Finnish Border Guard will gain new capabilities to monitor the movement of people near the Russian border. This has become possible thanks to the recent authorization of radio-technical surveillance.
The need to strengthen border control arose due to provocations by Russia security service involving migrants from Somalia and Iraq, whose mass movement was noticed at Finnish checkpoints at the end of 2023 and the beginning of this year.

Reportedly, the notifications will provide information about the start of an air raid, the location of restrooms, children's areas, auxiliary services at train stations and on trains, and other important information.

The Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation announced that it opened a case of illegal crossing of state border against three journalists who were filming reports in Kursk region, Russian agencies report.

It concerns CNN journalist Nick Peyton Walsh, hromadske journalist Diana Butsko, and "We are Ukraine" correspondent Olesya Borovyk, who were filming reports from the city of Suja, Kursk Oblast, after Ukrainian troops entered there.

FSS RF claims in the near future all three journalists will be declared internationally wanted.

Russian Telegram channels report that Ukraine, contrary to international law, is using chemical weapons in the Kursk region. The Center for Countering Disinformation(CCD) denied this information.
The reason for the use of chemical weapons is the alleged "impossibility of breaking through the Russian defenses."

The CCD emphasizes that Ukraine signed the Convention on the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons and strictly adheres to its obligations. In addition, Russian side does not provide evidence of the use of such substances by the Armed Forces.

Hackers of the Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine(GUR) attacked the servers of Russian TV channels, after which a number of TV companies broadcasted videos about the war in Ukraine.

As stated in the explanatory note, from now on, manufacturers of medicinal products won`t be able to place on the outer and inner packaging information about the unjustified advantages of the drug and other data that will contribute to its promotion on the market.

The requirement also applies to information about legal entities or individuals who aren`t manufacturers or owners of the registration certificate for the drug.

Users from Russia began to complain about problems in the work of Telegram, Viber and WhatsApp messengers. They also recorded failures in the operation of the Steam gaming platform, the Twitch streaming service, YouTube, Instagram, Discord and Skype social networks, the AppStore, the Wikipedia, numerous bank sites and mobile operators. DDoS attacks were named as the reason why.

Propagandists claim that the disease was allegedly caused by the pollution of the Dnipro River with the bodies of Ukrainian soldiers and the failure of the treatment facilities, the Center checked the epidemical situation with Kherson RMA and denied such disinformation.

In an attempt to convince people who left Ukraine because of the war not to return, Russia is preparing new propaganda materials. The National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE) reports a significant increase in digital payments in Ethiopia, with a 750% increase over the past five years, indicating a significant shift in the country's financial and economic landscape.

The government is prioritizing digital literacy to equip citizens with necessary skills for digital transformation, according to Director of Administration Hilary Namainja during the Digital Readiness Assessment Workshop in Mangochi.

Experts have estimated that the Kremlin spent approximately $50 million on disinformation and hybrid warfare efforts in Moldova in 2023. They expect this to double to $100 million in 2024.

This money is spent to bribe politicians, fund influencers, pay for advertisements, and for outright voter bribery.

While the Moldovan authorities have had some success in intercepting illicit money flows and restricting the licenses of Kremlin-linked TV and radio channels, disinformation continues to spread widely.

The Digital Malawi Acceleration Project (DMAP) under IDEA aims to enhance internet access and government service delivery through an initial $70 million grant, expected to grow to $150 million, and potentially mobilize $50 million in private sector financing.

The Malawi government has condemned the misuse of social media by individuals who create false pages, manipulate content, and spread misinformation. Minister of Information and Digitalisation Moses Kunkuyu expressed concern over the increasing instances of fake news.

Malawi police have seized mobile phones and laptops from 14 journalists at the state-run Malawi Broadcasting Corporation (MBC), suspected of running a fake Facebook account for false and anti-government stories, with press freedom groups accusing the police of invading their privacy.

The fake channel "Red Cross of Ukraine" duplicates most of the news from the official channel of the Ukrainian Red Cross, the organization writes. Administrators of the fake channel encourage people to leave their personal data in an online application in order to allegedly receive UAH 6,500 in monetary support.

While the global press has been reporting breathlessly on the first invasion of Russia since World War II, the Kremlin-controlled Russian media has been instructed to minimize the significance of Ukraine’s offensive and convince domestic audiences that the presence of Ukrainian troops inside Russia’s borders is the “new normal.”

This strategy has been all too evident on Russia’s federal TV channels throughout the past fortnight, with comparatively little coverage of Ukraine’s cross-border operation.

GoU adopted a law on the regulation of church organizations that have their headquarters in Russian Federation(RF). Churches suspected of cooperation with RF should be checked by selected commission of State Service of Ukraine on ethnopolitics and freedom of conscience(DESS), then are obliged to correct the situation, if not - lawsuit.

The Council of Europe has reacted to Russia-initiated criminal cases against journalists of Italian TV channel RAI, American TV channel CNN and Ukrainian correspondents. 

The "intimidation" of foreign journalists by the RF "amounts to censorship and is aimed at preventing public opinion from receiving information about ongoing operations," reads a statement on the Council of Europe's platform for the protection of journalism and the safety of journalists. 

Statement concerns Kursk region news, aired by journalists who allegedly violated Russian border.

A key part of the Russian campaign included bot accounts linked to the inauthentic Doppelganger network, which explicitly blamed Ukraine for the attack despite there being no evidence to back up this claim.

In the televised interview on August 20, Lukashenka(formal lider of Belarus) accused some post-Soviet states of what he called "unfair relations with Russia," specifically mentioning antigovernment protests in Kazakhstan in January 2022 that turned deadly after Kazakh President Qasym-Zhomart Toqaev invited troops of the Russia-led Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) to help him restore order.
Later on Belarusian diplomat in Astana was asked to meet authorities - Minister of Foreign Affairs.

indicator: ILI3 - Vulnerability of specific groups within the context / safety and dignity of people accessing information
justification:
Interview caused sharp reaction in Kazakhstan and other countries such as Armenia, where protesters pelted Belarusian Embassy in Yerevan with eggs and other produce and demanded diplomatic ties with Minsk be cut over Lukashenka's interview, in which he also criticized Armenia's shift westward.
"Who needs Armenians? Nobody. Let them develop their economy and rely on their own resources. What is France? Who is [French President Emmanuel] Macron? Tomorrow, when Macron is gone, everybody will forget about Armenians," Lukashenka said in interview.

Lukashenka's(formal lider of Belarus) interview came amid Ukrainian armed forces' incursion into Russia's Kursk region, which led to speculations in many post-Soviet countries that Russia could now call on the CSTO member states - Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan - to help it repel Ukrainian troops.

Journalist Andrey Kuznechyk of RFE/RL's Belarusian Service, known locally as Radio Svaboda, on August 21 marked his 1,000th day in prison on charges, he, his employer, and human rights organizations call politically motivated.
Kuznechyk, a father of two, was arrested on November 25, 2021, and initially sentenced to 10 days in jail on hooliganism charges that he rejected.
Subsequent charges included creating an extremist group were made secretly from acquaintances. Human rights groups in Belarus have recognized Kuznechyk as a political prisoner.

Polish security services have neutralized a sabotage operation orchestrated by Russia and Belarus that aimed to destabilize Poland, Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said on September 9. Saboteurs, operating from Belarus in cooperation with Russia, penetrated local and central government institutions, including state-owned companies implementing military contracts. Minister said that the Belarusian and Russian foreign services aimed to extort information, to blackmail individuals and institutions, and to wage a de facto cyberwar; cyberattacks have doubled since last year as well.

Amnesty International's Deputy Regional Director for East and Southern Africa, Sarah Jackson, has criticized the mass arrests and arbitrary detentions of Chadema party figures, supporters, and journalists in Tanzania, urging the authorities to respect people's rights to freedom of expression and association in the run-up to local government elections.

UNHCR and Senate President Pro Tempore Loren Legarda hosted a photo exhibit titled “Resilient Spirits: Capturing Courage, Celebrating Strength, Inspiring Inclusion - An Odyssey of Women and Girls in Finding Hope Away from Home.” The exhibit aimed to showcase the resilience of forcibly displaced and stateless women and girls, promoting rights-based solutions for their protection. During the launch, stakeholders including government officials, civil society, and the UN Country Team, pledged to enhance inclusion efforts for these vulnerable groups.

A Malian radio and television presenter remained in detention following comments he had made in March 2023 to the effect that the former Prime Minister Soumeylou Boubèye Maïga, who died in detention on 21 March 2022, had been “assassinated”. The presenter was arrested and detained on 13 March 2023 for simulation of an offence, criminal conspiracy, damage to the credibility of the State and crime of a racist and religious nature.

On 6 April 2023, a journalist was abducted by hooded gunmen in Bamako, before being released on 10 April 2023. Several actors, including the National Human Rights Commission26 and the Press House of Mali, have expressed concerns about acts committed against media professionals, including “extrajudicial” abductions, blackmail, threats, intimidation and arrests.

On 7 November 2023, one journalist was killed, another wounded and two others abducted in an attack by unidentified armed individuals on the road between Ansongo and Gao. The kidnappers reportedly demanded a ransom of 6 million CFA francs (about US$ 9,980) for the release of the two abductees.

Following six-day conflict that destroyed the homes of over 3,500 refugees living in Kakuma and Kalobeyei, IsraAID immediately launched an emergency assessment, training frontline workers from the refugee community to conduct the assessment and provide basic psychological first aid.

The World Food Programme (WFP) offered technical support to the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock Development by organising a "Training of Trainers" focused on the Right to Food and Food Systems Strategic Planning. This training, which reached 24 government officials and development partners from various levels, aimed to boost their skills in managing food systems and help localise them. Welthungerhilfe also contributed to this important training initiative, enhancing the participants' capacity to improve food security and system sustainability.

The World Food Programme (WFP) supported the Food Management and Trading Company Limited (FMTCL) in organising a training session on rice fortification. This training involved 30 FMTCL officials and covered key areas such as production, food safety, quality assurance, demand creation, and the nutritional benefits of fortified rice. The initiative aimed to improve the capacity of officials to promote fortified rice as a nutritious food option, ensuring enhanced food quality and health benefits for consumers.

Under the Local Infrastructure Support Project, the World Food Programme (WFP) provided technical assistance to the National Local Infrastructure Sector Assessment and helped revise the National Infrastructure Policy in Karnali and Lumbini Provinces. The project aims to enhance local governments' capacity to deliver accountable, inclusive, effective, and sustainable infrastructure services. WFP also offered both in-person and virtual technical support to 15 local governments, focusing on improving their infrastructure planning capabilities to better serve their communities.

justification: Due to flash flooding that occurred on the night of 9 September, when the Alau Dam collapsed wreaking havoc across MMC (Maiduguri Metropolitan Council) and Jere, the local telecommunications and electricity networks continue to be disconnected in some areas.

On 1 April 2024, a journalist was arrested and held incommunicado for several days by the Jubbaland Intelligence and Security Agency in Luuq District, Gedo Region. He was released on 8 April 2024 without having been charged or brought before a court. On 17 April 2024, another journalist was arrested and detained overnight by the National Intelligence and Security Agency at the Godka Jilicow detention centre after he had broadcast in-depth and critical reports on his social media channel.

The Palang Pracharath Party PPRP strongly denied the authenticity of an explosive audio clip allegedly featuring its leader General Prawit Wongsuwan expressing his desire to lead the country The party claimed the clip was an AI-generated fake The controversial recording was aired on the popular program Inside Thailand alongside three other voice clips purportedly involving Prawit

Scammers posing as police officers have been targeting residents, resulting in a spike in calls to the Nonthaburi City Police Station. The scammers, pretending to be law enforcement, claimed they needed to verify bank accounts, causing public confusion. They alleged the victims were involved in illegal money laundering and requested ID cards and for the victims to add the officers online for further verification.

Financial and digital literacy education activities utilizing the Bank of Uganda curriculum are ongoing for targeted refugees in ten refugee settlements. According to WFP, by end of August, 32,746 out of the targeted 83,751 households had completed training aimed at imparting knowledge and skills on financial management.

Ethiopia's Digital 2023 Global Overview Report shows 20.86 million internet users as of 2023, with 6.4 million actively engaged on social media. This burgeoning social media landscape, comprising 5.1% of the population, is a trend reflected in 30.7% of internet users accessing at least one platform.

Ethiopia has a growing social media presence, with 20.86 million internet users as of 2023, and 6.4 million actively engaged on social media. This trend is reflected in a broader trend, with 30.7% of internet users accessing at least one platform. The Ethiopian Media Authority warns of the threat of hate speech and false information to individual safety and societal welfare, arguing that social media platforms have not adequately addressed this issue.

Human Rights Watch reports that Mozambican police have committed widespread abuses against journalists and civil society activists, potentially affecting their work ahead of October 9, 2024 elections, as authorities have rarely investigated complaints of harassment, threats, physical assault, and arbitrary arrest and detention.

As Namibia's Presidential and National Assembly elections approach, the country faces challenges in regulating social media due to the spread of misinformation, as most companies are not within their jurisdiction, according to Information Deputy Minister Modestus Amutse.

Namibian social media has been flooded with deceptive AI-generated content aimed at influencing elections. This includes images, videos, and audio clips that spread falsehoods about political candidates and parties competing for support in the upcoming elections.

Ethiopia has launched a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) facility to improve data exchange in its digital public infrastructure. The facility, launched in Addis Ababa under Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's guidance, was developed in collaboration with the Information Security Network Administration.

The May 2024 Index reveals significant differences in cybersecurity risk levels across African countries. Egypt ranked highest, followed by Namibia and South Africa. Ethiopia and Zimbabwe had the highest risks. Other African countries, including Angola, Maldives, Kenya, Ghana, Mauritius, Morocco, Uganda, and Nigeria, continue to face cybersecurity challenges.

The Minister of Transport and Communications, Mateus Magala, stated that 73% of the Mozambican population lacks internet access. He emphasized the need for innovative, environmentally friendly solutions involving the private sector to provide internet to all, highlighting the need for a paradigm shift.

Human Rights Watch reports that Mozambican police have committed widespread abuses against journalists and civil society activists, potentially affecting their work ahead of October 9, 2024 elections. The authorities have disrupted opposition party campaign meetings, broken peaceful protests, and detained journalists and activists for extended periods without charge.

On December 14, journalist João Chamusse, a scathing critic of the current government and co-founder of Ponto por Ponto, was found dead outside his Maputo home. Police arrested his neighbor Nelson Jone Mulanda after finding Chamusse's clothes. The motive for the murder remains unknown, and his phone and laptop were missing at the time of the incident.

Ethiopia's state-run telecom firm, Ethiopia-Telecom, reported that the country's internet users have surpassed 41 million, despite a growing number of mobile subscribers. This growth is part of the government's Digital Ethiopia 2025 digitization initiative, according to Frehiwot Tamiru.

The Ethiopian Government's Digital Ethiopia Strategy 2025 aims to achieve 70% digital literacy by 2025, but current statistics show significant gaps, with only 3% of Ethiopians using mobile money, 14% using digital services, and fewer than 20% familiar with ATMs and mobile money agents.
